items.title: Artificial/Ancestral: Black Theatre and the Question of AI
items.excerpt: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these tec...
items.fullDescription: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these technologies have arrived without history, entering an empty landscape awaiting innovation. Yet Black theatre has long grappled with questions of representation, embodiment, archives, intellectual inheritance, collective memory, labor, and futurity. Rather than asking simply what AI can do for Black theatre, this issue invites contributors to consider what Black theatre reveals about AI itself: its assumptions, limitations, aspirations, and consequences. Volume 4.2 of the Black Theatre Review seeks essays, interviews, case studies, pedagogical interventions, archival investigations, artist statements, and process reflections that place Black theatre and performance studies in critical conversation with artificial intelligence and related technologies. We are particularly interested in work that moves beyond questions of adoption, utility, or rejection toward deeper examinations of power, ethics, governance, memory, embodiment, and knowledge production. We welcome contributions from scholars, artists, archivists, educators, practitioners, dramaturgs, designers, and cultural workers whose engagement with these questions emerges from both theory and practice. The issue is organized around five interrelated areas of inquiry. These themes are offered not as rigid categories, but as points of departure for further investigation. Taken together, these areas encourage contributors to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a site through which questions of labor, memory, embodiment, governance, spirituality, and future-making can be reconsidered. AI, Labor and Extraction: The beneficiaries of AI systems, whose labor makes them possible and required forms of accountability when Black creative work becomes data. Possible points of investigation may include: The labor of artists whose knowledge underlies any AI-readable record and what ethical stewardship of that labor requires. Generative AI in dramaturgy, script analysis, and design workflows, and models of artist-led intentional integration. Archives, Memory, and Black Theatre Histories: How do AI systems shape, distort, recover, or fail to capture Black theatrical histories and modes of remembering? Possible points of investigation may include: Digitization and AI-training projects involving Black theatre collections and their assumptions about what counts as trainable data. AI-assisted archival misreadings, flattening, erasure, and historical distortion. Embodiment, Liveness, and Performance: What happens when embodied, communal, and improvisational performance practices encounter technologies built on prediction, simulation, and abstraction? Possible points of investigation may include: Case studies of AI in the classroom, rehearsal hall, or production process. The complementary offerings of embodied, ensemble-based theatre training to university-wide AI adoption. Relatedly, how do such offerings get recognized, funded, or institutionally protected? Ancestral Intelligence, Spiritual Knowledge, and Black Futures: Understanding AI as a knowledge system entering into conversation with much older Black diasporic traditions of intelligence, memory, and futurity Possible points of investigation may include: AI as ancestral intelligence, or Black diasporic traditions of pattern recognition, forecasting, memory, and knowledge transmission. How do Black diasporic understandings of knowledge, memory, inheritance, ritual, and collective survival shape the technological futures we imagine? Refusal, Governance, and Alternative Technological Practices: Forms of resistance, opacity, governance, and the possibilities of misuse Possible points of investigation may include: How Black artists are bending, breaking, or refusing AI against its intended use. Teaching against technological inevitability. Photograph, Visual Media, and Digital Project Documentation tBTR welcomes photographic, visual media, and digital project documentation that illuminates the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We encourage submissions featuring productions, rehearsals, classroom projects, design processes, digital or hybrid performances, archival initiatives, community-based projects, and artistic experiments that engage the themes of this issue. Submissions may include production photography, design renderings, screenshots, interface documentation, archival images, process documentation, and other visual materials that help narrate how artists, scholars, educators, and institutions are critically engaging AI and related technologies. All submissions must include the project or production title, names and roles of key collaborators, location, creator and/or photographer credit, date, and a 2-3 sentence description explaining the work's relationship to the issue's focus on labor, archives, embodiment, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, ancestral knowledge, refusal, governance, or Black futures. Contributors are responsible for securing all necessary permissions and reproduction rights prior to submission. Please contact the managing editor for additional information. Book Reviews, Performance Reviews, and Notes from the Field, and Multimedia Works In addition to scholarly articles, tBTR seeks book reviews, performance reviews, multimedia works, illustrative case studies, and notes from the field that engage the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We are particularly interested in contributions that document pedagogical experimentation, archival initiatives, institution-building efforts, production processes, dramaturgical and design practices, community engagement, and artist-led technological interventions. We also welcome reflections on the ethical, political, and aesthetic questions surrounding AI, including issues of labor, extraction, memory, embodiment, governance, ancestral intelligence, resistance, and alternative technological futures. Submission Guidelines The last date for submissions is September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT. Please refer to the tBTR website for specific article section guidelines. Manuscripts must be submitted in Microsoft Word using standard formatting (1-inch margins, double-spaced, single-column layout, and 12-point Times New Roman font). Please include an abstract and a 150-word author biography with your submission. All submissions must include footnotes and a bibliography and must fully comply with The Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), using the notes and bibliography system. Please do not use the author-date citation system or another style guide. Please upload your complete manuscript through the journal's online submission portal via the website. Early submissions will receive preference in the review and publication process.

items.excerpt: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT Univ...
items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. items.fullDescription: The erotic is a point of infinite signification, a navel in humanity’s symbolic circuit. However, despite its resistance to formalization, it is always in the process of not being written. As Octavio Paz insists, the erotic is a metaphor indelible to the human. As such, it is unsurprising that the manifestations of the erotic in subjective embodied experience are variable and correspond to equally plural treatments of it across the academic panorama. This diverse archive is bound by certain distinguishable threads, in terms of the potentiality of the erotic, its singular relation to language, and to the sphere of sexuality.

items.fullDescription: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. items.fullDescription: If American mass media is an ecosystem, we cast the press as predators, and the celebrity as their prey. We envision the reporters grouped in a posse, arranged for an ambush. Camera flashes crack as they capture their quarry. By now, these perceptions have become truisms that obscure our own role as consumers in a matrix of violence, spectatorship, and stardom. If we condemn the paparazzi for their alleged violence, we also continue to revise and revisit their heyday in the age of print media. This seminar seeks papers that explore how violent desire—of the spectator, the press, the star – shaped the profusion of tabloid and true crime print culture across the Americas.

items.fullDescription: Conference online (via Zoom) CFP: What makes us happy and content in our life? Some people may point to fabulous fame, fortune, or money. Others may argue that interpersonal relationships are the key to happiness. But what if someone is alone? Is loneliness truly disastrous? Are there any benefits of loneliness? Can loneliness become an epidemic? To address these questions, this event focuses on a wide range of specific issues. We are interested in exploring all aspects of loneliness, both in the past and in the present-day world. The conference is intended as an interdisciplinary event. Hence, we invite researchers representing various academic disciplines: sociology, psychology, psychiatry, philosophy, anthropology, gender studies, literary studies, theatre studies, film studies, consciousness studies, social policy, cognitive sciences, and history, among others. The aim of our conference is to provide opportunities for researchers from a range of disciplines and countries to share their research, create an academically challenging and productive space for discussion, and enable them to establish long-lasting, ever-growing scientific networks and contacts with professionals worldwide. We welcome submissions from both experienced scholars and young academics at the beginning of their careers, as well as doctoral and graduate students. We also invite individuals interested in participating in the conference as listeners, without giving a presentation. The topics of the conference include but are not limited to the following suggestions: 1. Loneliness and Society loneliness and social relationships (in families, marriages, partnerships, workplaces, etc.)? loneliness and war loneliness and illness loneliness and self-isolation, social distancing loneliness among children loneliness among seniors the lonely crowd loneliness in urban spaces loneliness as an epidemic loneliness and pandemic loneliness and social exclusion (social class, racism, gender factors, educational status) loneliness and social media (Facebook, Instagram, etc.) 2. Loneliness and Culture loneliness in different parts of the world loneliness and religions loneliness and initiation rituals lonely communities abandoned nations expelled minorities loneliness and digital cultures / virtual communities the cultural taboo of solitude vs. hyper-individualism migrant loneliness and diaspora experiences 3. Individual experiences loneliness during self-isolation, quarantanne, loneliness as a state of mind loneliness and emotional isolation loneliness and depression loneliness and shame creative loneliness loneliness as a rest situational loneliness existential loneliness loneliness, aloneness, and solitude the commercialization of loneliness (the "rent-a-friend" industry, monetized companion apps, dating algorithms, and AI relationships) synthetic companionship & AI (digital intimacy, dating algorithms, and robotic care) 4. Literature and Arts loneliness in literature, film, theatre and visual arts lonely artists aesthetics, spaces, and narratives of isolation (e.g., in pop culture, life-writing, and architecture) Please submit abstracts (no longer than 300 words) of your proposed 20-minute presentations, together with a short biographical note, by 18 September 2026 to: lonelinessconference@gmail.com

items.excerpt: Poster session at the conference "Entangled Normativities in the Digital Transformation: Technology, Society and the Shaping of Law" Present your research where law, technology and society are being negotiated. How much technological change can normative orders gover? How do law, ethics and social norms change themselves once their creation, mediation and...
items.fullDescription: Poster session at the conference "Entangled Normativities in the Digital Transformation: Technology, Society and the Shaping of Law" Present your research where law, technology and society are being negotiated. How much technological change can normative orders gover? How do law, ethics and social norms change themselves once their creation, mediation and enforcement become digitally mediated? No single discipline settles these questions. With a poster you discuss your project at the centre of the programme, alongside scholars and practitioners working on exactly these questions: Möllers (HU Berlin), Nassehi (LMU Munich), Paulus (former Justice of the German Federal Constitutional Court), Schlögl-Flierl (German Ethics Council), Foblets (MPI for Social Anthropology), Vec (University of Vienna), Hansen (State Data Protection Commissioner of Schleswig-Holstein) and Bubnys (European Commission), among others. What you get:Viisibility in front of leading scholars and practitioners rather than in a parallel session; substantive feedback in conversation plus a short written comment on your abstract; a citable peer-review process; networking with doctoral researchers from across Europe; free attendance on both days. Potential poster publication on our website. Who can apply. Doctoral researchers in law, science and technology studies, sociology, political science, philosophy and ethics, history, computer science and engineering with a societal research question, design, communication and media studies, and further or interdisciplinary fields. What matters is not your disciplinary label but your contribution to the relationship between normativity and technology. Your stage of doctorate is irrelevant: proposals, early outlines and first interim findings are as welcome as work nearing completion, and practitioners pursuing a doctorate alongside their work are invited too. From big picture to concrete cases. We welcome conceptual and foundational contributions (theories of normativity under technological change, legitimacy and the rule of law in digital governance, the interplay of legal, ethical, social and technical norms, automation of norm application, interdisciplinary methodology) as well as specific, applied and empirical work (the AI Act and data protection law in practice, platform regulation, digital administration and courts, predictive policing, health data, technical standardisation, sustainability, and case studies of individual technologies, authorities, decisions or regulatory processes). Please relate your contribution to one of the three guiding questions: (1) To what extent is technological change amenable to normative and in particular legal governance? (2) To what extent must normative orders, above all the law, themselves change? (3) What potentials and risks does the technological transformation of normativity and law entail? How it works. Each session opens with lightning talks: max. 90 seconds and one slide per poster; questions are taken at the posters rather than in the plenary. Day 1 (German, 5 November): pitch session 4:15-4:35 PM, poster session from 4:35 PM into the Apéro riche. Day 2 (English, 6 November): pitch session 11:20-11:40 AM, poster session 11:40 AM-12:35 PM before lunch. Posters are on display both days; your poster language determines your pitch day. Peer review and selection. Each anonymised abstract is assessed independently by two members of the review committee, with divergences discussed in the committee. Criteria: thematic fit, academic quality, originality, clarity, and potential to spark discussion in an interdisciplinary audience. All applicants receive a briefly reasoned decision by early October 2026; interdisciplinary submissions are read by reviewers from different fields. Poster. A0, portrait, printed and brought by you. Recommended: two or three key messages, body text at least 24 pt, a large self-explanatory title, and more visuals than running text - your poster should be understandable within a few minutes even when you are not next to it. Questions: lst@sot.tum.de. We look forward to your application!

items.fullDescription: This virtual seminar takes its inspiration from Saidiya Hartman’s citation of the Greek etymology of the word chorus : “to dance within an enclosure.” For Hartman, the chorus also furnishes a paradigm for thinking—to play on Jean-Luc Nancy’s notion—Black (non)being singular plural. In Wayward Lives , Hartman suggests that any of the minor figures can stand in for the others, not as a claim of homogeneity, but rather as a contention that their singularity can be read as paradigmatic of waywardness—in its queer heterogeneity—in general. The chorus of black femme and queer youth is thus at once a singular plurality and a plural singularity as they make beautifully riotous lives within the enclosure of social death.

items.location: Houston, Texas · American Comparative Literature Association
items.excerpt: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literatur...
items.fullDescription: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literature as a major field of inquiry, discussions of literary circulation have often privileged routes that pass through metropolitan centers, emphasizing translation into dominant European languages, global publishing networks, and institutions located in the Global North. Yet literary works have long traveled through alternative circuits that connect regions of the Global South directly, producing histories of exchange that challenge center-periphery models of cultural transmission. This seminar invites papers that examine literary relationships among Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, SWANA, Oceania, and other locations within the Global South. Such relationships may emerge through translation, political solidarity, migration, anti-colonial movements, publishing networks, educational institutions, shared aesthetic projects, or indirect forms of influence. They may also involve moments in which Northern institutions, languages, or markets facilitate, mediate, redirect, or constrain South-South encounters, raising questions about whether these exchanges can ever be understood as entirely autonomous. Rather than treating the Global South as a unified category, the seminar seeks to explore its internal heterogeneity, asymmetries of power, and competing visions of solidarity. How do texts travel between Southern contexts? What historical, linguistic, and political conditions make these encounters possible? What role do translators, publishers, periodicals, archives, and digital media play in creating or sustaining South-South literary networks? How might these circulations reshape concepts such as influence, comparison, translation, reception, or worldliness? We especially welcome papers that interrogate the implications of South-South literary exchange for the study of World Literature itself. If literary circulation is not exclusively organized through Northern centers, what alternative maps of World Literature become visible? Can South-South networks offer different ways of imagining literary value, canon formation, and global comparison? By foregrounding overlooked routes of circulation and exchange, this seminar aims to reconsider how World Literature is conceptualized and to illuminate the multiple worlds through which literature moves. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: South-South translation; comparative studies across the Global South; Cold War and Non-Aligned literary networks; postcolonial and decolonial approaches; migration and diaspora; publishing and periodical cultures; digital literary circulation; transregional modernisms; indigenous and vernacular exchanges; reception studies; archives of literary solidarity; and new theoretical approaches to World Literature.

items.fullDescription: “We are now in the middle of a deep and decisive moment towards a more disciplinary, authoritarian kind of society,” says Stuart Hall in his speech for Human Rights Day in 1979 (78). He proceeds to explain the components and manifestations of this “crisis,” which eventually morphs into a drive for more “Law and Order” (79). If that was the middle, are we at the end of the crisis? Our daily experiences prove otherwise, as the drive for more Law and Order keeps us in a chokehold. We seem to be in a perpetual global crisis in which we watch global systems of justice like international law and the International Criminal Court deteriorate in front of our eyes, while capitalist and genocidal systems globally continue to thrive and strengthen their hold.

items.title: ACLA Online Panel: Case Studies in Feeling: Toward New Theories of Emotion Across Media
items.excerpt: Emotions continue to attract critical attention across disciplines. Scholars have noted the growing prominence of emotion in media, politics, and internet culture, which some describe as an "emotionalization" of social life (Yanacek 2026). Over the past three decades, emotion theory has provided a multidisciplinary lens for understanding literary and cult...
items.fullDescription: Emotions continue to attract critical attention across disciplines. Scholars have noted the growing prominence of emotion in media, politics, and internet culture, which some describe as an "emotionalization" of social life (Yanacek 2026). Over the past three decades, emotion theory has provided a multidisciplinary lens for understanding literary and cultural texts, phenomena, and movements. Brian Massumi's distinction holds that emotion is socially coded and contingent on language, whereas affect is a pre-linguistic, asignifying intensity that exceeds discourse's capacity to fully capture it (1995). Sara Ahmed reframes emotion as social and relational rather than private, arguing that emotions "stick" to bodies and objects through repeated circulation, accumulating or losing affective value in the process (2004). Historians such as Barbara Rosenwein instead approach emotion diachronically, investigating the sanctioned "emotional communities" of different historical periods and how their norms of feeling and expression changed over time (2006). These frameworks are not fully reconcilable. For example, Massumi's model of pre-personal intensity has been challenged by critics such as Ruth Leys (2011), who question whether a truly pre-social affect is theoretically or empirically defensible. This tension among circulation, historicization, and the limit of pre-linguistic feeling remains a live and generative debate in the field. Game studies extend this inquiry into interactive media, asking scholars to account for procedure, system, and player agency alongside representation when studying emotion in play and design. Meanwhile, recent advances in facial recognition and artificial intelligence have pushed machines "from analytical processors to emotionally perceptive entities," if not to emotional entities themselves (Slimani 2026). These approaches resist treating emotion as ahistorical, private, or apolitical. Studying feeling as a legitimate, theorizable object reveals how power operates through affect, opens texts to modes of engagement beyond decoding, and invites us to reconsider the boundaries of the human, including where those boundaries fall in relation to nonhuman and machine forms of feeling. This panel invites papers that develop, test, or complicate existing theories of affect and emotion through close case studies, rather than merely applying them. We welcome submissions on any literary or cultural form, including but not limited to novels, poetry, drama, film, and video games, from any historical period and geographical region. This panel will be held online. Please go to https://www.acla.org/seminars, log into your ACLA account, find the panel, and submit your paper proposal by clicking the submit button.

items.title: Across Borders, Across Texts: Echoes, Revision, and Rewritings in Black Literature
items.location: University of Houston, Houston, Texas. · American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA)
items.excerpt: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literatur...
items.fullDescription: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literature across centuries, dating back to the antebellum. For instance, "Flight to Canada" by Ishmael Reed and "Kindred" by Octavia Butler; Harriet Tubman's "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" and Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad, published almost two centuries after Incidents; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Percival Everette's 2024 "James." These examples reinforce the notion that newer Black literature echoes, borrows, and imitates seminal literatures. This seminar thus seeks to investigate how Black literary and cultural productions have imitated other, earlier literary productions, even across genres and geographical boundaries-like what the editors of the anthology The Negro Caravan (1944) called "a sort of literary inbreeding which causes Negro writers to be influenced by other Negroes…" Even Kwame Anthony Appiah recently aver that "the history of art is the history of people borrowing and adapting techniques and tropes from earlier works." We seek papers that-using fictional and non-fictional Black writings and art-connect the past to the present-papers that explore "imitation," "influence," and "intertextuality" as central to Black literature and Black arts. Guiding questions to consider include, but are not limited to: What literary traditions have endured across generations, and how have they survived? What forms of continuity exist across Black literary history-Plantation to post-bellum literary and cultural productions, Africa to the Diaspora, across centuries, etc.? How do Black writers create new meanings from older texts? What role does memory play in Black literary traditions? How do contemporary writers preserve or challenge earlier literary traditions? How does Black literature reinvent its own past? What histories continue to shape Black literary expression? How do questions of race, identity, and freedom evolve across Black literary history? What earlier genres continue to influence Black literature today? How does Black literature balance tradition and innovation? What can earlier Black literature teach us about contemporary Black writing? Submit abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/defa99b9-6a8d-41ab-835d-2f1281fc3640 Session modality: Strictly in-person. Questions? Email: saadewumi@wisc.edu

items.title: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature (ACLA 2027, online)
items.excerpt: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world...
items.fullDescription: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world literature theories, considered as an effective tool to rethink contemporary authorship issues, it encourages at the same time proposals that aim to identify and deepen conceptions of the author coming from understudied historical and geographical contexts, thereby broadening the cultural horizon of Western reflections on the subject. Indeed, we are mostly used to considering authorship as a romantic notion, strictly linked to the paradigm of genius and individuality, the authority of which was famously questioned by twentieth-century literary theory-relying primarily on such celebrated thinkers as Barthes and Foucault-before re-emerging in the post-structuralist era. However, other historical periods and cultures have not necessarily applied the same theoretical paradigms nor followed the same critical trajectory (think about collaborative or anonymous authorship in the Middle Ages, as well as the lack of the rhetoric of genius in most Far Eastern literary traditions, to give just a few non-exhaustive examples). In our opinion, it is therefore important to rethink the notion of authorship in the light of these divergent traditions, especially to ensure a more complex and multi-focal approach to it in an increasingly globalized literary context. Even though theories of world literature have profoundly transformed the ways in which the critical field of literary studies is currently understood, we argue that, in fact, the crucial category of authorship has received comparatively little sustained attention within this debate. While effectively highlighting how substantial changes in the literary system have simultaneously reconfigured the author as a global cultural agent whose visibility depends on complex networks of publishing, mediation, and institutional recognition, the world literature perspective has less frequently questioned the Western theoretical framework of authorship as a productive and individual stance. We therefore suggest that merging genealogical reflections on authorship with world literature studies could help to make the latter much more inclusive and global, rather than a mere framework of Western concepts superimposed on the literatures of the rest of the world. We welcome papers in English, French, Italian or Spanish. Possible topics include: - authorship in world literature theories; - the intersection of authorship, postcoloniality, and the global literary market; - twentieth-century theories of authorship and their global afterlives; - pre-modern, indigenous, and non-Western conceptualizations of the author; - multilingual, exilic, diasporic, and transnational authorship. Please submit your proposal through the ACLA's online paper portal by September 22, 2026 (an abstract of no more than 1,500 characters and a short bio-bibliography). Once your account has been created, simply click on the "propose a paper" button available at the following link: https://www.acla.org/ seminar/263adf13-fe6c-4fc3- 95f7-87083b14e3f9. Should you encounter any difficulty, please do not hesitate to contact the seminar organizers (giovanni.salvagninizanazzo@ parisnanterre.fr; federico. ristagno@phd.unict.it). Notification of acceptance will be sent by December 1, 2026.

items.title: William S. Burroughs as a Problem, Not a Subject
items.excerpt: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over th...
items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

items.title: TALKING DIFFERENTLY: MARGINALISED WOMEN AND THE FORMS OF INTERSECTIONALITY IN SOUTH ASIA
items.excerpt: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www....
items.fullDescription: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e Marginalised women in South Asia are read for what was done to them, far less often for what they made. This seminar asks what comparative literature can do about that. Intersectionality has become the default grammar for writing about marginalised women in the region. It arrived from a particular genealogy - Black feminist jurisprudence in the United States - into a region that had theorised compounded subordination for a century under other names: Phule on caste and women's education; Ambedkar on endogamy as the mechanism reproducing caste through control of women; Pandita Ramabai; Uma Chakravarti's Brahmanical patriarchy; Gopal Guru's claim that Dalit women talk differently; Sharmila Rege's Dalit feminist standpoint. Whether the import clarifies or flattens that inheritance is contested. Nivedita Menon argues that intersectionality serves states and donor agencies better than feminist politics; Sunaina Arya and Anandita Pan reply that the fault is citational, not conceptual. That argument has run almost entirely in social science. Our premise is that intersectionality is a diagram - a crossroads, a grid, a set of axes. Literary forms do not behave like diagrams. They work through voice, genre, meter, silence, obscenity, laughter, ritual and untranslatability. What does intersectionality look like as a reading practice rather than a taxonomy of identities? Where does form outrun the grid, and what should replace it - standpoint, assemblage, repertoire, abundance? Three provocations frame the seminar. First, the arithmetic of injury: criticism here tends to produce a tally of wounds, in which the Dalit, Adivasi, Muslim, trans, disabled or displaced woman is legible chiefly through what was done to her. Charu Gupta shows this figure has a history: in colonial Hindi reformist print the polluting "vamp" gave way to the deferential sufferer, Surpanakha displaced by Shabari, while the Dalit virangana of 1857 offered a rival image that never took. Following Gupta, Anjali Arondekar on archival abundance over loss, and Shailaja Paik on Tamasha performers who turn vulgarity into leverage, we welcome papers that read craft, expertise, pleasure and the ordinary. Second, marginality is not virtue. Tanika Sarkar's work on the Hindu wife as ground of cultural nationalism, and on women's agency inside right-wing movements, refuses to assume that subordination guarantees a critical position. We want dominant-caste women's self-writing - Rashsundari Debi's Amar Jiban - read alongside rather than apart from Dalit testimonio, and the complicities an axis model hides. Third, translation. Most of these texts do not exist in English. Bama's Karukku and Challapalli Swaroopa Rani's Telugu poems reach the Anglophone academy through an apparatus - glossary, preface, caste footnote, anthology - that turns literature into evidence. Swaroopa Rani's "Water" registers not only the village/wada line but the gradations within it, leather-worker and weaver. The grid has grids inside it, and translation is where they flatten. Topics might include, but are in no way limited to: the genre problem in Dalit women's testimonio; Dalit feminist poetry read as theory; the manufacture of the suffering woman in colonial print and the counter-archives that failed; nineteenth-century women's self-writing and its caste unconscious; women as agents of majoritarian politics; sung and seasonal repertoires as authorial economies rather than folklore; Adivasi women's poetry and the politics of script; landays and Afghan women's oral forms; testimonial method in Kashmir; plantation labour and memory in Sri Lanka; Muslim women and the meme as a genre of gendered communal violence; trans and hijra life-writing at the caste intersection; devadasi, Tamasha and courtesan archives read for abundance; caste in North America and Gulf labour circuits; translation as method. We invite papers on any South Asian language, region, period or diaspora. Researchers and Faculty Members at every career stage are welcome, including independent researchers and those working outside the Anglophone academy, and papers that argue against the seminar's premises are equally welcome. To submit: proposals go through the ACLA portal, not to the organisers directly. Visit https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e and use the "Propose a Paper" button. Current ACLA membership is required. Deadline 22 September 2026. We'd like to have you in person, please mention your preferred mode- ONLINE/IN PERSON along with the abstract. Enquieres: nandinigayen006@gmail.com; tamanna0602@gmail.com

items.excerpt: In his book, Bioinsecurities: Disease Interventions, Empire, and the Government of Species (2016), Neel Ahuja's theory of "the body as a transitional theater of imperial warfare" explores how the control of human and nonhuman bodies proliferated the expansion of empire over the 19th century to the present. Despite the growing hegemony of biomedical contro...
items.fullDescription: In his book, Bioinsecurities: Disease Interventions, Empire, and the Government of Species (2016), Neel Ahuja's theory of "the body as a transitional theater of imperial warfare" explores how the control of human and nonhuman bodies proliferated the expansion of empire over the 19th century to the present. Despite the growing hegemony of biomedical control, there have always been and continue to be significant moments of resistance and agency in which marginalized (colonized/Indigenous) communities have challenged or reformulated/redefined the concepts of body, disease, and health. This seminar seeks to foster a discussion in order to understand how the body can be read as a transnational figure of resistance and refusal both in the 19th century and today. Through various disciplines on the subjective and untold experiences of the body, health(care), and illness, we hope to shed light on the fluctuations in imperial medical frameworks and decolonial epistemology that pose alternative narratives-both realist and speculative-about biomedical discourses of health, gender and sexual normativity, disability/deficiency, hygiene, humanness, life/death. We are interested in questions such as: How are illnesses phrased, represented, imagined in marginalized communities? How is the effectiveness of care and therapies a scientific, ethical, and cultural problem? How can the medicalized body-or the body that is made into a site of changeability and "treatment"-become a speculative site entangling place, race, gender, and sexuality? This seminar welcomes papers that take on interdisciplinary approaches to literature and other forms of cultural production such as film, print culture, and music that engage with the theme from the 19th- 21st centuries across the world. We are especially interested in lesser-known materials and understudied communities. Topics of interest include but are not limited to: Narrative medicine from all types of media Bioethics Biopolitics and governmentality Mental health and literature, art and media studies Limitations of medical or pharmaceutical knowledge Medicalization of health/illness Marginalized bodies in medicinal knowledge (queer, disabled, racialized, female) Community/Immunity Pandemic and contagion Aging studies and end-of-life care, childcare/youth studies Utopia/Dystopia/Ecotopia Toxicity and Waste Trauma and memory studies Supernatural bodies, cyborg and alien "others", metamorphosis and transformation (Digital) post-life, afterlife studies, martyrdom Animal studies, Post-humanism To submit an abstract, please go to: https://www.acla.org/seminar/82ccd196-900f-482d-aac6-3b983a0957b2. Click the "Propose a Paper" button.

items.fullDescription: Over the last two decades, we have seen a surge of scholarship at the intersection of Food Studies and New Materialist theory. Thinkers like Elspeth Probyn (2000; 2016), Jane Bennett (2010), Annemarie Mol (2021; 2024), and Kyla Wazana Tompkins (2024) explore the diverse ways in which edible matter acts on our bodies, wills, and dispositions, in multilayered entanglements that involve water, minerals, fungi, bacteria, plants, as well as human and nonhuman animals. These material-discursive networks urge us to rethink not only our notions of agency but also our ways of being, knowing, and relating.

items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. ACLA Paper Submission link: https://www.acla.org/cfp/2b603883-5d9b-44ae-a485-c732ba80d4bf/submit-paper. Papers can be submitted until September 22, 2026 .

items.fullDescription: This call is for panelists to present on an approved in-person NeMLA 2027 panel on "The Gothic Servant." While the Gothic has long been associated with monsters, haunted houses, unstable hierarchies, and hidden knowledge, the servant's specific connections to the genre's core dynamics of space, affect, and plot have been critically undertheorized. Yet Gothic narratives fundamentally depend upon servant figures to produce narrative tension, mediate hidden knowledge, and expose the instability of domestic, social, and political order. This panel therefore positions the Gothic servant not as a supplementary character but as a central Gothic mechanism and epistemological problem worthy of scholarly attention and analysis. We invite panelists to consider the following types of questions: In what ways does the servant function as a Gothic mechanism, producing narrative tension, circulating forbidden knowledge, and exposing the instability of domestic and class order? How do the servant's social and/or affective roles (as caregiver, confidante, observer, jailer, etc.) shape Gothic plots and complicate power hierarchies within Gothic narratives? How does the servant's structural invisibility produce, rather than merely reflect, Gothic preoccupations with spectrality, repression, identity and/or power? Topics may include but are not limited to: servants as uncanny, spectral, or monstrous figures; servants as central to Gothic plot and narrative structure; servants, secrecy, and forbidden knowledge; race, coloniality, and servitude in imperial and postcolonial Gothic; invisibility and the Gothic politics of service; servant figures in contemporary Gothic; and the afterlives of Gothic servant characters in adaptation and other media. We welcome papers on servant characters in Gothic texts from the mid-nineteenth century to the present, from any geographical area. Whereas digital accessibility is a technical standard that ensures that digital tools, documents, and platforms are usable by everyone, regardless of ability.

items.fullDescription: What strategies can paper ephemera teach us in the digital age? This panel invites conversations by writing instructors, educators, poets, and artists exploring the work that happens at/within the margins of writing. Both literally and figuratively, we take an expansive scope to the term “margins,” imagining not only the writing that appears on the space of the printed page, but writing that would normally be scrapped, discarded, remixed, or ephemeralized. This can include digital ephemera, such as “disappearing” messages in Instagram or other communication services. At another angle: margins can also mean the liminality of writing, the furthermost edges of what’s often standard and visible.

items.fullDescription: Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā , another name for Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS), is a comprehensive body of knowledge which has been accumulated over millennia. Indian Knowledge Systems encompasses philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, medicine (Ayurveda), government, ecology, the arts, and sustainable living. It is based on books such as the Vedas , Upanishads, Puranas , and treatises like the Arthashastra , Charaka Samhita , and Sushruta Samhita . This Knowledge systems place a strong emphasis on interconnection, moral behaviour, and harmony with the natural world - principles embodied in ideas such as Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family).

items.fullDescription: Panel Proposal for the NeMLA Convention, Newport, RI, March 6–9, 2027 Planetary crises—climate change, toxic pollution, biodiversity loss, and energy transition—are profoundly uneven in their distribution. Their material consequences are shaped by infrastructures of class, race, colonial histories, state power, and global capitalism. Increasingly, literary, artistic, and cultural texts across the world foreground these asymmetries, framing ecological crisis not only as environmental catastrophe but as a question of justice: Who breathes polluted air? Who profits from green transformation? Who consumes melting ice? Who bears the social and environmental costs of planetary change?

Yet the fantasy of constructed or quasi-human life long predates modern computing and robotics. Classical and pre...
items.fullDescription: "Did I request thee, Maker?": Contemporary Cyborgs and Androids and Their Pre-Modern Antecedents Contemporary speculative fiction is saturated with androids, cyborgs, artificial intelligences, and technologically engineered forms of sentience. Yet the fantasy of constructed or quasi-human life long predates modern computing and robotics. Classical and pre-modern literature repeatedly imagines artificial beings, animated matter, virtual persons, mechanical servants, enchanted automata, and forms of life that blur the boundary between the human and the non-human. This panel invites papers that place contemporary representations of manufactured or technologically mediated beings in dialogue with their classical or pre-modern antecedents. Possible pairings might include science fiction, film, television, comics, anime, or video games alongside texts from antiquity through the early modern period. What conceptual, philosophical, theological, or aesthetic frameworks for artificial life emerge in pre-modern literature? How do earlier traditions of animation, embodiment, enchantment, or mechanical simulation anticipate contemporary debates surrounding AI, consciousness, labor, gender, race, affect, or personhood? While Frankenstein remains a central touchstone for discussions of artificial life-and itself invokes Paradise Lost as part of that genealogy-this panel is especially interested in less frequently discussed genealogies and archives. What ancestors to the android or cyborg might be found in Ovid's Metamorphoses, the works of Shakespeare, medieval romance, alchemical traditions, Jewish mysticism, Islamic philosophy, Buddhist narrative traditions, or other non-Western pre-modern texts? Possible topics may include automata and animated objects; artificial or manufactured bodies; alchemy, magic, and technological imagination; pre-modern theories of mind, soul, and consciousness; race, gender, and constructed embodiment; virtuality, simulation, and illusion; labor and mechanical life; monstrosity and the posthuman; game studies and worldbuilding; and theological or philosophical anxieties surrounding creation itself.

items.fullDescription: In the definition given by Podnieks, matrifocal literatures are written and narrated by mothers in the first-person or limited third-person voice, rendering maternal identity and experience from subjective perspectives. Such narratives (re)value the significance and meaning of maternal figures in cultural, social, and national arenas, and often contest or negotiate traditional ideologies of the “good” mother as self-sacrificing, nurturing, and sexless with her antithesis, the “bad” mother. In the last few years, we have seen the rise of matrifocal writings published to break taboos about previously silenced reproductive experiences, create a sense of community, support, and care, and, overall, empower people.

items.fullDescription: Haryanvi Dalit theatre occupies a highly marginalised position within the broader landscape of Indian theatre. It may aptly be described as “the marginalised among the marginalised,” as it has remained largely excluded from both mainstream theatre studies and Dalit cultural historiography. Haryanvi Dalit Swang theatre was active long before the Dalit Panther Movement, but it received little attention due to its lack of publication and translation into English. This book seeks to recover, document, and critically examine the neglected legacy of Haryanvi Swang, with particular emphasis on its Dalit traditions and practitioners, thereby contributing to a more inclusive understanding of Indian theatrical heritage.

items.excerpt: TITLE: Language Learning Beyond the Classroom: Virtual Exchanges, Platforms, and AI MODALITY: Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. CHAIRS: Liana Ewald (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Dagmar Jaeger (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ABSTRACT: This session explores the growing role of virtu...
items.fullDescription: TITLE: Language Learning Beyond the Classroom: Virtual Exchanges, Platforms, and AI MODALITY: Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. CHAIRS: Liana Ewald (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Dagmar Jaeger (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ABSTRACT: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interactions in language, literature, and culture courses. In recent years, many instructors have experimented with new ways of connecting students with speakers, authors, and communities beyond the classroom: Teletandem exchanges, Zoom conversations with writers and artists, commercial conversation platforms, and AI conversation partners. These exchanges can open up forms of communication and cultural contact that are difficult to create in a traditional classroom, especially for students who may not have access to study abroad or regular interaction with speakers from other linguistic and cultural contexts. At the same time, these tools raise important questions. What kinds of communities do these exchanges create? What changes when conversation becomes mediated through platforms or AI? How do students respond to the differences between speaking with another person and interacting with an AI system designed to simulate one? What happens when intercultural exchange becomes something organized and mediated by commercial companies, especially when those relationships may at times raise questions about inequality or exploitation? The session is especially interested in presentations grounded in classroom experience, as well as broader reflections on the pedagogical and theoretical questions raised by these forms of virtual and AI-mediated exchange. Possible topics include current and emerging forms of virtual exchange, AI-mediated interaction, commercial platforms, the changing relationship between human and technological forms of communication, and the pedagogical, cultural, and ethical questions these developments may raise in the years ahead. DESCRIPTION: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interaction in language, literature, and culture courses. items.excerpt: The term "transgressive fiction" was coined in 1993 by LA Times columnist Michael Silverblatt to describe a loosely related coterie of authors in the '80s and '90s whose writing has "violation at its core: violation of norms, of humanistic enterprise, of the body." items.fullDescription: The term "transgressive fiction" was coined in 1993 by LA Times columnist Michael Silverblatt to describe a loosely related coterie of authors in the '80s and '90s whose writing has "violation at its core: violation of norms, of humanistic enterprise, of the body." Silverblatt's preliminary "sketch" of the genre's leading voices was primarily American, almost entirely Anglophone, and exclusively white. Since its coinage both the term and the archive it describes have widened to include both a more diverse set of contemporary Anglo-American authors and a broader set of transnational and transtemporal texts. In both academic and popular contexts "transgressive fiction" has come to loosely describe Anglo-American authors from Samuel R. Delany to J.G. Ballard, non-Anglophone writers like Ry? Murakami and Virginie Despentes, and historical antecedents ranging from Petronius's Satyricon to the writings of the Marquis de Sade. The para-academic provenance of "transgressive fiction" as a term and its liberal application, especially by non-scholarly readers, to a wide range of culturally and historically distinct texts make it a problematic, yet perhaps fruitful, term for academic, historicist scholarship. This panel proposes both to interrogate the risks and benefits of "transgressive fiction" as a scholarly rubric, as well as a bid to further widen its archive by considering neglected texts from across space and time that might, however loosely, be identified as transgressive fictions. Proposals might ask: Why (not) use "transgressive fiction" over alternative terms like "blank fiction" (Annesley, Caveney, Young), "aggressive fiction" (Hume) or "queer experimental fiction" (Bradway)? What do we, as scholars or readers, wish to find transgressed by such fiction? Is the heterogeny of transgressive fiction's archive part of its transgressive appeal? What neglected texts ought to be considered in the lineage of transgressive fiction? What contemporary texts resonate with its organizing principles? Submissions accepted until September 20th, 2026. Submit at https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22718. Ya'el Z. Frankel yzfrankel@gmail.com Doctoral Candidate University of British Columbia (Vancouver)

items.title: Silences as Resistance in Public Narratives
items.excerpt: Silences as Resistance in Public Narratives Silence is generally seen as something to surmount: we break silence; we give voice to silenced stories; we speak out against injustice. But silence can be a powerful mode of expression in its own right. There is a history of silent protest. Silence can reject dominant expectations or refuse to offer up a story...
items.fullDescription: Silences as Resistance in Public Narratives Silence is generally seen as something to surmount: we break silence; we give voice to silenced stories; we speak out against injustice. But silence can be a powerful mode of expression in its own right. There is a history of silent protest. Silence can reject dominant expectations or refuse to offer up a story for voyeurism, appropriation, or commodification. It can push reader-listeners to listen for something wordless, to play an active role in striving to understand, and simultaneously to recognize the limits of their ability to understand another person's trauma. Silence is rarely ever singular. This seminar, building on successful past seminars about the roles and limits of narrative silences, examines how silences function as forms of resistance to injustice and trauma. It asks: how can we use silences (as creators or as audiences) to create new spaces-spaces of care, of resistance, of justice? How do we listen to what silences have to say-in fictions, testimony, activism, artistic forms of witness, our classrooms and institutions? How can audiences attend to silence in ways that promote structural change? Participants may choose to address some of the following questions: How do the forms of silence change between public narratives (e.g. testimony or activism) and works of art and literature? How can we theorize silence as a narrative framework? How do we hold the tension between listening to silence, on one hand, and the necessity of speaking out against injustice, on the other? How do historical and geographical contexts change the types or effects of silences that strive to oppose injustice? How can we keep from homogenizing silences and attend to them in their specificity and situatedness? Papers on all genres, media, geographical contexts, and languages welcome. Please submit 200-word abstract and bio through the NeMLA portal to Kelly Minerva and Lisa Propst.

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention - "Empowering Communities" March 6-9, 2027 | Salve Regina University, Newport, Rhode Island Roundtable Title: Writing and Wellbeing: A New Urgency for Human-Centered Composition Pedagogies Primary Area / Secondary Area: Rhetoric & Composition / Pedagogy & Professional Modality: In person only Chair: Miranda Lutyens, University of Massachusetts Amherst College is a time of excitement and novelty, but it can also bring about anxiety and uncertainty. Those unsettling emotions have been on an upward trend in recent years, with a host of factors - the fallout of the pandemic, social media's curation of idealized lives, and existential fears relating to climate change, generative AI, and political turmoil - raising concerns about the wellbeing of students. The college writing classroom has a long history of offering compassion through creative (and even countercultural) approaches to teaching and learning. This included affirming the rights of linguistically marginalized students to their own language, as well as efforts to keep struggling writers in school to keep them out of the Vietnam War. As we collectively face new urgencies, this roundtable session invites participants to share research projects and instructional practices that consider college writing classrooms as affective and embodied spaces. Recognizing concerns such as instructors' emotional labor and under-resourced writing programs, the session primarily focuses on putting forward innovative approaches to making writing instruction responsive to students' experiences in increasingly uncertain times. Insights gained from critical teacher research on human-centered pedagogies are particularly welcome, as are contributions from all levels of writing instruction, including first-year composition, writing in the disciplines, writing support for graduate students etc. The goal of this roundtable is for both participants and attendees to leave with expanded perspectives on how the college writing classroom might offer students more pleasure and new possibilities - to reimagine a more salutary relationship to writing, to engage with the written word in more personally meaningful ways, and to gain a greater awareness of themselves and others. The roundtable also aims to offer practical strategies for enacting - or at least experimenting with - new classroom practices. Submission Deadline: September 30, 2026 Please submit abstracts via the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22547 Convention information can be found here: https://www.nemla.org/convention.html
