items.title: Cripping Literary and Cultural Studies: Neurodivergent and Mad Methodologies
items.excerpt: Critical disability studies and the medical humanities have generated growing interest within cultural and literary studies in the past decade. Yet scholars in these fields tend to engage with disability and illness either thematically, examining their representations in literary and cultural productions, or rhetorically, tracing how they inflect the very...
items.fullDescription: Critical disability studies and the medical humanities have generated growing interest within cultural and literary studies in the past decade. Yet scholars in these fields tend to engage with disability and illness either thematically, examining their representations in literary and cultural productions, or rhetorically, tracing how they inflect the very form of these productions. Rarely do such approaches ask how disability and illness might transform criticism itself, that is, how neurodivergent or mad cognition might become a critical resource, transforming the ways we read, analyze, and inhabit literary and cultural studies. This panel invites papers that take up this question, exploring what new methodologies neurodivergence and mental illness-including, but not limited to, autism, ADHD, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, OCD, PTSD, and depression-can generate. How might neurodivergent and mad ways of thinking and being-in-the-world produce innovative, crip approaches to literary and cultural analysis that refuse sane- and neuronormative standards? Such a project finds grounding in Arseli Dokumaci's concept of disability-as-method, "a creative approach through which research methods are informed by, modeled after, and tailored to the situated knowledges of disabled people" (Activist Affordances, 11). It also resonates with Robert McRuer's call to challenge "straight composition, with its demand for composed and docile texts, skills, and bodies" (Crip Theory, 171), as well as with Jack Halberstam's notion of low theory, a voluntarily undisciplined mode of knowledge that defies the linearity and restraint of established academic discourse (The Queer Art of Failure). We welcome papers that generate or point toward new critical approaches grounded in neurodivergent and mad cognition and cripped methodologies. We particularly encourage submissions in which such cognition is presented as an embodied epistemological standpoint where neurodivergent or mad experience shapes the work from within, rather than serving as a structuring metaphor.

items.title: Between Mobility and Mobilization: Lessons from Cultural Production
items.excerpt: In what ways can literary mobilities provoke questions about social movements and forms of resistance in the current global order? Mobility is not simply the physical navigation of spaces, but an embodied and affective act with deep socio-cultural and political significance. items.fullDescription: In what ways can literary mobilities provoke questions about social movements and forms of resistance in the current global order? Mobility is not simply the physical navigation of spaces, but an embodied and affective act with deep socio-cultural and political significance. Literary and cultural work that represents varied forms of mobility can reveal contradictions between the exercise and assumption of agency and uneven historical and social conditions of restriction. Whether mobilities are framed as environmental, diasporic, colonial, or decolonial, they pose questions about material and symbolic conditions of power that dictate who can move and in what ways. This session welcomes proposals on subversive mobilities in cultural production to interrogate the connections between mobile subjects and wider mobilization efforts, resistance movements, protest cultures, and expressions of dissent. In investigating the links between mobility and mobilization, this session seeks to engage a wider conversation about the relationship between movement and resistance. Central questions this session will address include: How do different narratives-literature, film, graphic and visual arts, or other forms of storytelling-connect mobilities to activism and resistance movements? How do narrative forms participate in protest cultures? How do mobilities articulate political claims? This session welcomes papers with interdisciplinary approaches to narrative forms and textual cultures.

items.fullDescription: I want to be accepted by society…live in a world I don't have to hide in…make choices without being in constant fear of them destroying me or the ones I care about." (Ada, liberated TanakX5 robot, on her hopes and dreams. Alex + Ada, Book 11) Many contemporary and recent speculative fiction texts interrogate the questions of "making kin" with companion species, including the companions humans might engineer and build to keep us company. In her Staying with the Trouble, Donna Haraway proposes reknitting the current order to address Capitalocene-generated problems of overpopulation and overconsumption. To survive, humans must extend their care and loyalty to other inhabitants of our shared planet, and co-construct knowledge -sympoeisis-with them. Haraway includes part-biological cyborgs in the potential so-called symbionts with whom humans should co-exist, but does not expressly include fully non-biologic, mechanical partners in her analysis. Yet, as part of the thought experiment enacted by speculative fictions of manufactured fellow beings, Haraway's prescription might be expanded to encompass sentient partners whom humans engineer and manufacture to keep themselves company. This roundtable invites papers interrogating speculative fiction solutions for expanding kinship relations to sentient non-biologic companions, whether embodied robots, virtual companions, or other. In other words, how does a particular creator of an imagined world envision expanding Haraway's Chthulucene era of "oddkin" to included fully artificial as well as natural companion species? And how do these artificial companions fare, that is, are the humans in their worlds able to embrace their right to equal standing and accord them rights?

items.fullDescription: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal economic infrastructure that marginalizes the local communities, and even after independence from the colonial power, the trade relations remain that of a colonial appendage. Similarly, the upkeep of the digital sphere is not without its economic and environmental hazards. Anibal Quijano (1928-2018) a Peruvian sociologist, talks about the plight of this expansion for resources in his book, On the Coloniality of Power. He says: …the contemporary scientific community, insists on destroying the conditions for life on the planet. So, both the movement of the most subjugated people in this world, those who would not be able to exist if they sold their means of subsistence, and those who realize that if all this comes to an end no one will be able to survive, come together in a shared analysis. 359 He stresses on the role of the communities who've resisted the colonial and postcolonial measures to protect their land, water, and air over the years. It shows how the communities have more of a lateral structure which allows for debate and discussions as opposed to the hierarchy of the colonial administrative infrastructure. This panel seeks to garner discourse around the digital world's ambivalent nature of enhancing global communications and generating jobs at the cost of endangering local communities. Questions, challenges, and possible solutions for a community-oriented resistance will be among the many concerns discussed at this panel. Submit on NeMLA's website: Submit an Abstract

items.fullDescription: This roundtable seeks to put in conversation Blue Humanities from around the world, exploring how literature, cultural texts, and film can inform, reveal, or create new ideological perspectives on water. Informed by Blue Humanities, as well as a global movement to protect water's right to flow and be free from pollution (Ecuador Constitution of 2008: Rights of Nature, Policy Brief: Water rights in Chile, Canada Water Act of 1985, among others), this timely roundtable connects directly with NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention theme of Empowering Communities. As the theme specifies, cultural knowledge serves as a source of empowerment, and literature, cultural texts, and film are primary ways that cultural knowledge is shared amongst communities. These cultural artifacts can be powerful, informing the public, bringing together younger and older generations, and inspiring people to take action, conserving water, protecting its right to be free from pollutants, and reminding us all that we live, together, on the Blue Planet. This roundtable aims to explore stories that empower communities to protect water's right to flow. How literature, film, and cultural texts inform or reveal ideological perspectives from around the world and how those stories connect with political action are of great interest. We invite (among others) presentations related to the transnational exploration of Blue Humanities, with a particular interest in the intersection of literature, ideology, and policy making. items.fullDescription: Despite possessing intersecting histories and languages, Latin American studies and Latinx studies have historically been treated as separate fields of study. This panel seeks to spark a dialogue between fields by exploring themes of transhemispheric and archipelagic solidarity in Latinx and Latin American literature and media. Throughout the past and present century, how have Latinx and Latin American media-literature, film, art, or other forms-constructed expressions of community in dialogue with each other? How do works from Latin America reverberate in Latinx cultural productions, and how do Latinx cultural productions influence Latin American media? How do these intersections challenge our notions of the borders, both theoretical and physical, between both territories? Literature, film, art, and other forms have a long history as modes of cultural preservation and empowerment, especially in Latin American and Latinx communities. What can we discover about these communities and their agency through a borderlands approach to Latin American and Latinx studies? While submissions from Latin American and Latinx studies will be considered, papers explicitly engaging in solidarities between the two disciplines will be prioritized. Submissions in English, Spanish, and Portuguese are welcome. Interdisciplinary projects are also encouraged.

items.title: The Classroom as Counter-Archive: Place-Based Pedagogies of Community Empowerment
items.location: Salve Regina University. Newport, Rhode Island · NEMLA
items.excerpt: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in produ...
items.fullDescription: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in producing their own interpretations of the cultural and spatial memory they share with their forebears. We draw inspiration from courses in which students articulate their personal, familial, and communal relationships with the tangible and intangible spaces of the city they inhabit: from their own homes to the streets they traverse daily, the buildings, neighborhoods, and monuments they encounter, and the individual and social practices that animate them. Setting their lived experience against the historical archives that purport to represent them, students produce analytical descriptions of urban space. Their work collectively assembles a shared repository of cultural memory - a "counter-archive" that weaves together place-based learning, immigration histories, and autobiographical narrative. In classrooms of diverse composition, this work empowers along more than one path. Immigrant students illuminate the place of their communities within the urban social fabric, while others discover-in their own projects and in those of their classmates-insights that transform how they perceive the city and their own identities in relation to it. We invite educators across languages, periods, and disciplines to share pedagogical projects and activities-assignments, archives, community-engaged work, digital repositories, creative and testimonial writing-that treat teaching as a practice of empowerment. We especially welcome contributions that reflect on the theory of change behind their work: when does a classroom project produce agency, and how do we know?

items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. Drawing on approaches from cultural studies, postcolonial theory, sociolinguistics, and intersectionality, this session seeks to understand how literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic narratives stage the tensions between marginality and belonging, strength and vulnerability. Proposals engaging with environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous studies, as well as diaspora and migration studies are strongly encouraged. We also welcome submissions drawing on gender and queer studies, memory and trauma studies, digital humanities, or other interdisciplinary frameworks within the humanities. We welcome proposals of 250-300 words, in French or English, submitted by September 30.

How do we as language pedagogues lean in on culture and interculturality as a source of strength and empowerment in our programs, in order to collaborate with all stakeholders and foster innovation in our language programs? In the embattled environment that is the American university of 2026-2027, and particularly for the language and humanities programs fighting for enrollments and their own survival, how do we empower ourselves and our students in the language classroom, encouraging active engagement in extracurricular activities, and bringing cultural knowledge to bear in community-based outreach and programs? In what ways does interculturality take on new meaning in today's world, in the language classroom, and in academia? This roundtable will explore innovation and empowerment in the language classroom and in language learning communities, where culture is the key to empowerment and innovation. We will reflect on new ways for creating community, creating spaces of innovation, and connecting the classroom to the larger world outside the classroom and to the university through culture and collective action. We welcome presentations that showcase novel pedagogical ideas, lived experiences, and creative practices in language teaching and cultural engagement.

items.fullDescription: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses are often kept to general education requirements and could be perceived as peripheral to students' professional training. Within such environments, Humanities faculty must navigate not only broader disciplinary challenges but also institutional cultures that may misunderstand or underappreciate the field's contributions. This roundtable invites faculty working in specialized institutional contexts to reflect on how they sustain and advocate for the Humanities amid these pressures. How do instructors articulate the intellectual, ethical, and professional value of Humanities study to students primarily focused on career-focused pathways? What pedagogical or curricular strategies have proven effective in demonstrating relevance to disciplines such as engineering, nursing, or business? Alternatively, how have faculty members built collaborations with colleagues across fields to integrate Humanities perspectives into specialized curricula? Participants will also consider how they engage multiple audiences-students, faculty peers, and administrators-to communicate the significance of Humanities education. By sharing concrete strategies, institutional experiences, and models of interdisciplinary partnership, this discussion aims to highlight adaptable approaches for maintaining the visibility and importance of the Humanities in specialized settings. Ultimately, the roundtable seeks to reassert the Humanities as essential to professional education. This roundtable is part of the Northeast Modern Language Association conference, which will take place between March 6-9, 2027 in Newport, RI. Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. 250-word abstracts for participation in this roundtable are welcome, and they can be submitted through this website: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/login

items.fullDescription: Call For Papers - NeMLA 2027 Panel -- Supporting the Well-Being of Students and Instructors in a Transitional Time Northeast MLA 2027: March 6-9, 2027 Panel Title: Supporting the Well-Being of Students and Instructors in a Transitional Time Modality: Virtual Only: All presentations will be delivered via Zoom regardless of whether the presenters are in-person Format: 3-4 presentations/papers, 15-20 minutes per presenter The past few years - which could be described as part of a larger cultural, political, and economic flash point -- have created true challenges for higher education. This transitional time has put pressure on all parties of our postsecondary community, as seen in the reported mental health challenges of undergraduates and the high rates of burnout amongst faculty and support networks in the sector (Mowreader; Pourasadollahi and Vincenti; Liu). In addition to these post-pandemic stressors, a host of broader concerns are also impinging on the postsecondary environment (see "The Trends Report" for one discussion). How can we empower our community - defined through instructors, students, and/or support services -- during such a transitional moment? This session will create a dialogue that touches on any of the following: -discussions/studies of interventions and/or articulations of already established practices in supporting the well-being of students and/or instructors; -the reflections of students, instructors, and/or support networks on the challenges of and responses to our contemporary moment. These challenges can include: the impact of budget cuts on postsecondary contexts, the fallout of declining academic freedom in the classroom, the impact (positive or negative) of Gen AI on the well-being of our community, the discord between instructor expectations and the reality of students. items.fullDescription: This panel takes its organizing provocation from John Ashbery's Other Traditions (2000), his Charles Eliot Norton Lectures that recover six largely overlooked poets as formative, eccentric aesthetic presences. We propose that queer literary practice has faced and flirted with parallel challenges, demanding that practitioners orient towards literary heritage that is damaged, incomplete, or institutionally suppressed without either abandoning, misrepresenting, wantonly mourning, or converting suffering into false affirmation. How do writers hold open a queer futurity that depends on what didn't survive? How do you theorize the erotic charge of reading and writing across historical time? These are not merely theoretical puzzles, and this panel claims that poets and writers have been solving them in practice-in essays, lectures, hybrid prose, and the criticism embedded in poetry itself-with a rigor and suppleness that literary scholarship has been slow to take seriously on its own terms.

items.fullDescription: Palestine and the Challenge to German Studies Northeast Modern Language Association (NeMLA) annual convention Newport, Rhode Island March 6-9, 2027 Submission Deadline: 30 September 2026 through the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22528 Recent work in and around German Studies (Younes and Al-Taher; El Bulbeisi; Özyürek; Moses; Salehi) argues that the erasure of Palestinian identity in Germany is tied to deeper national tensions: How the country remembers its past, how it talks or avoids talking about race, what kinds of political speech are treated as acceptable, and how it confronts histories of imperialism and genocide. Moreover, scholars (Thompson and Tuzcu; Ragab; Daher) have documented how major institutions in Germany have been engaged in a wave of repression of ethnic minority communities, targeting Palestinians, other people of color, and Jewish anti-Zionists. This scholarship demonstrates how such pressures influence which voices, histories, and political positions are treated as legitimate within the field of German Studies, and which ones are marginalized. This panel invites contributions that explore how German Studies has begun or has struggled to engage with the significance of Palestine and Palestinian life, not only in contemporary German culture, politics, and literature, but within the discipline's own structures. While scholarship on Holocaust memory culture, as well as on multidirectional memory and migrant memory archives, has broadened the field's understanding of how Holocaust memory circulates and how migrant communities navigate its demands, recent work, such as articles by Catlin, Kundnani, and Rosenbrück in the New German Critique special issue "German Memory Politics at a Crossroads" (2026) provides evidence of the limits of these frameworks and the political pressures that shape them. Rather than challenge the centrality of Holocaust memory itself, this panel aims to examine how it is mobilized to foreclose other histories of violence, displacement, and coloniality, and how this foreclosing makes it difficult to integrate anti-imperialist, antiracist, and decolonial approaches that would situate Germany within broader histories of imperialism, colonial violence, and genocide. Palestine makes these dynamics visible by revealing how debates about memory shape disciplinary boundaries, how racialization and political speech determine scholarly legitimacy, and how exclusions are reproduced even within critical frameworks. This panel welcomes contributions that examine where Palestine appears, where it is actively excluded, and how these patterns expose German Studies' unresolved tensions around race, German colonial histories, and the politics of knowledge production. The goal of this panel is to open a conversation about how German Studies might expand beyond memory-centered approaches toward more globally attuned, anti?imperialist, and decolonial analytical frameworks. Topics include but are not limited to: · Intersectional decolonial feminist frameworks and praxes · Critiques of white Western imperial feminism · "Pinkwashing" and "homonationalism" to justify colonial violence and dehumanize Indigenous communities · The role of anti-Palestinian racism in mainstream anti-immigrant backlash and far-right political actors · Scapegoating of Muslims as the new Nazis in the theory of "imported anti-Semitism" (Özyürek) · Germany's colonial and neocolonial relationships to the broader region of West Asia · Integrating Palestinian perspectives into pedagogy, curriculum, and study abroad advising · Courses and lesson plans that include the Nakba and its continuity · German Studies and BDS/academic boycott · The "Historikerstreit 2.0" and attacks on "postcolonialism" · The history of East German solidarity with Palestinians · Student and faculty support in campus organizing for Palestine solidarity, and institutional and departmental barriers Abstracts: Please submit 300-word abstracts by 30 September 2026 though the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22528 For questions, please contact the panel organizer Maria Grewe (mgrewe@jjay.cuny.edu).

items.title: Beyond Hegemony: Masculinities in World and Comparative Literature
items.excerpt: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. We welcome papers addressing, but not limited to: Comparative constructions of masculinity across world literatures Masculinity and migration, diaspora, or displacement Literary representations of fatherhood, mentorship, and communal responsibility Masculinities in Global South literatures Masculinity and environmental or ecological communities Masculinity, memory, and post-conflict reconstruction Queer and non-hegemonic masculinities in world literature Masculinity and cultural resistance under authoritarian regimes Masculinity, religion, and collective belonging Masculinity and affect in contemporary global fiction

items.title: International Workshop “The Golden Age of Rural-Urban Migrations? Grassroots Perspective on Global Phenomenon 1930s – 1980s”
items.excerpt: In the mid-20th century, the world remained deeply divided - both politically and economically. The Iron Curtain, colonialism, and economic backwardness marked various boundaries. Yet in this divided world, the same process could be observed in various places: migration from rural areas to cities, and global urbanisation. Although this phenomenon has acco...
items.fullDescription: In the mid-20th century, the world remained deeply divided - both politically and economically. The Iron Curtain, colonialism, and economic backwardness marked various boundaries. Yet in this divided world, the same process could be observed in various places: migration from rural areas to cities, and global urbanisation. Although this phenomenon has accompanied humanity ever since cities first emerged, from the 1930s onwards - and particularly after the Second World War - there was an unprecedented acceleration: the second, after nineteenth-century urbanisation, such a rapid and irreversible social change. During the workshop, we aim to examine this change from a grassroots perspective, focusing primarily on human experience - the 'lives' of those at the centre of migration processes, interwoven with political and economic contexts, as well as global change - the 'system' with its geopolitical and economic mechanisms. The workshop, therefore, aims to analyse the processes by which 'ordinary people' enter urban, culturally heterogeneous social environments in various parts of the world. The global revolutionary transformation observed between the 1940s and 1970s affected ways of working, communicating, moving about and consuming, resulting in fundamental social changes. We believe that, despite specific contexts, this shared global experience of 'becoming urban' and/or 'remaining rural' can be identified, compared and summarised. We therefore wish to highlight the agency and actions of 'ordinary people' within these global processes and analyse them from a microhistorical perspective - drawing on biographical, local and intergenerational perspectives. We are interested in the origins of urban values and norms that we now take for granted, within politically and economically diverse systems. We encourage you to focus, amongst other things, on the functioning of the family, education, work, the consumption of goods and media, spatial and social mobility, discrimination and racism. We invite researchers from various academic disciplines (including history, sociology, anthropology, migration studies, and economics) to submit proposals for presentations that fit within the framework outlined above and address one or more of the following topics: ? migration to cities in individual biographies and intergenerational experiences ?mechanisms of migration to cities and transnational/transcontinental biographies (particularly between socialist and capitalist countries) ?the impact of policies and ideologies on migration experiences ?the relationship between horizontal and vertical social mobility: mechanisms of advancement or degradation; emancipation through migration ?mechanisms for creating and maintaining social hierarchies, practices of discrimination ?social mobility and shame in rural-urban migrations ?mechanisms and models of migration: chain migrations, commuting, migration networks ?means of communication and transmission of information ?rural-urban migration and gender order We particularly encourage you to submit papers on your ongoing research and research projects. Abstract (up to 250 words) and a short bio of the author should be sent by 1 October 2026 to the address rural.urban.biographies@gmail.com The notification of acceptance will be sent in the second half of October 2026. Participants of the workshop will be asked to share working versions or extended abstracts of their papers (3-5 pages) no later than the end of January 2027. The organisers will provide accommodation and board during the workshop. There will be no participation fee. We are delighted to announce that the keynote talk at the workshop will be delivered by Professor Ewald Fire (Eberhard Karls University of Tübingen), author of the book Ein Hof und Elf Geschwister. Der stille Abschied vom bäuerlichen Leben in Deutschland, which won the Deutscher Sachbuch Preis for the best non-fiction book of 2023! The workshop is part of the research project Globalising Upper Silesia. Migration from Rural Areas to Cities in the Global North, South and East ("Oberschlesien transkontinental: Land-Stadt-Migrationen im globalen Norden, Süden und Osten / Górny ?l?sk transkontynentalnie. Migracje ze wsi do miast na Globalnej Pó?nocy, Po?udniu i Wschodzie"), a joint project between the Institute of History at the Jagiellonian University and the Institute of History at Ruhr University Bochum, supported by the Polish-German Science Foundation from 2025 to 2028. Organisers: Marcin Jarz?bek (JU Kraków) Andrzej Michalczyk (RUB Bochum) Zofia Strzy? (JU Kraków)

items.fullDescription: From its founding ideals framing rights as tied to individuals to many of the ‘myths that made America,’ such as the self-made man, ideas of individualism are deeply entrenched in the culture of the United States. Yet at the same time, the US has also always understood itself as a particular community: as a city upon a hill, a melting pot, a more perfect union. As such, the United States has been established on a seeming paradox, forming ‘out of many, one.’ More recently, this previous consensus has become increasingly brittle, with fragmentation, polarization, hyper-individualism, and loneliness on the rise—as some would argue: again.

items.fullDescription: Despite the international prominence of Stanisław Lem and, more recently, Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher , Polish science fiction and speculative literature remain strikingly underrepresented in English-language scholarship. items.fullDescription: Public Humanities invites submissions for the upcoming themed issue Memorial Culture in Public Art, which will be guest edited by Rebecca Friedman and Alex Lichenstein. The deadline for submissions is October 15, 2026. Description Memorial Culture in Public Art invites submissions that examine the role that art of all kinds - ephemeral public art installations, performances, sculptures, murals, or permanent state-issued monuments - can play in the public's understanding of the past, present, and future. We ask contributors from a multitude of disciplines and from multiple global perspectives to consider how public arts can serve as collective mnemonic inspiration. We invite contributions from academics, public scholars, memory activists, and artists and creatives of all kinds, to explore the role of public art as a form of resistance as it contributes to collective, place-based memory in the face of forces from political ideology and spiritual expression to gentrification and cultural obliteration. Submissions can consist of academic articles, artistic interventions, interviews, dialogues, or other forms. Regardless of format or genre, contributors should engage with questions that include: How have regimes around the globe and across time, whether autocratic or democratic, created-or destroyed--narrative sites of collective memory in public spaces? How can individuals and groups intervene to transform nationalistic, colonial, or dominant narratives through their re-telling and/or transformation of art in public spaces? How can - and have in the past - individuals, groups, communities, neighborhoods, and even nations use(d) art, performance, and display to resist the power of erasure and cultural amnesia? How can public art help usher in a more equitable future based on reconstituting social memory? The current moment witnesses many struggles over memory, as emergent constituencies demand more accountability from public memorial culture while myriad regimes seek to obliterate it. This issue of Public Humanities seeks fresh and innovative approaches across time and spaceto consider these and other conundrums of memory activism and commemorative public art. The editors are especially interested in contributions from and/or about the Global South and the postcolonial world. By engaging the past through its present material and aesthetic manifestations, this issue of Public Humanities will use a host of disciplinary frames to explore how art and commemoration in public spaces open up a window onto how humans navigate space and time through artistic imagination, creativity and expression, and how collective remembering reflects and shapes our contemporary moment. Submission Guidelines Submissions should be written in accessible language for a wide readership across and beyond the humanities; see How to Write for Public Humanities. Articles will be peer reviewed for both content and style. Articles will appear digitally and open access in the journal. All submissions should be made through the Public Humanities online peer review system. Authors should consult the journal's Author Instructions prior to submission. All authors will be required to declare any funding and/or competing interests upon submission. See the journal's Publishing Ethics guidelines for more information. Contacts Dr. Rebecca Friedman | friedmar@fiu.edu Dr. Alex Lichtenstein | alichtens@gmail.com Questions regarding peer review can be sent to the Public Humanities inbox at publichumanities@cambridge.org.

items.fullDescription: "That Sounds Funny": CFP for ALA "Music and the American Literary Imagination" symposium The American Humor Studies Association (AHSA) invites submissions for a proposed panel for the American Literature Association (ALA) 2027 symposium "Music and the American Literary Imagination," to be held January 28-30, 2027, in Nashville, TN. For hundreds of years, humor has been an indelible element of American popular music as well as literature. This AHSA-sponsored, non-guaranteed panel seeks proposals that consider the connections between American humor, American music, and American literature. We invite submissions on any genre, period, or place, including papers that explore the fuzzy boundaries of what it means to be "American." We are especially interested in presentations that examine humor practices in the American South; for example, proposals might consider the use of humor in Southern rap, children's author Shel Silverstein's role in shaping the "outlaw country" sound, or the recent rise of right-wing "humorists" in Nashville. Together, the presentations constituting this panel will explore the pitfalls and possibilities of the imbrication of music, humor, and American literary culture. Please send a 250-word abstract and a brief biography by October 15, 2026, to AHSA Vice President Benjamin Schwartz at bs8959@princeton.edu. All panel participants must be AHSA members before the ALA conference opens on January 28, 2027. The Constance Rourke travel award is available for graduate students on a panel. The award varies between $100 - $300 (depending on AHSA funds and the number of applicants) to help defray the cost of attending conferences with AHSA-sponsored panels. We also remind everyone that AHSA has in place a mentoring program to help emerging scholars prepare an essay for publication. Presenting at ALA can be the first step to being published.

items.fullDescription: European Comic Art Special Issue 'Francophone Graphic Narratives / Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance' European Comic Art invites proposals for a special issue on 'Francophone Graphic Narratives/Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance'. This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its many forms - political, cultural, institutional, and aesthetic - and how they forge practices of resistance and dissent. The bande dessinée is a medium that subverts hierarchies and blurs boundaries. Long regarded as the lowly offspring of literature and the visual arts, comics have since been legitimised by scholars and artists demonstrating their capacity to engage with complex sociohistorical, political, and cultural topics. This 'Ninth Art' now occupies an increasingly important place in university classrooms, academic publications, and public discourse alike. Its multimodal features - panel layout, gutters, framing, braiding, and complex interplay between text and image - allow comics to stage and challenge authority in formally distinctive ways. This aesthetic vantage point makes comics a powerful medium through which to bring displaced, excluded, and silenced narratives into view. From Chantal Montellier's impressive four-decade oeuvre of political cartoons and graphic novels contesting racism, misogyny and totalitarianism to Jessica Oublié's Peyi an nou , which provides a counternarrative to state discourse on the BUMIDOM, the bande dessinée has often served to undercut official rhetoric. This special issue of European Comic Art seeks articles that examine how Francophone bandes dessinées engage with dominant institutions and discourses from theoretical and pedagogical perspectives. How do comics represent power and powerlessness? How do they respond to hierarchies that exist in various settings and communities? How do they decentre and challenge 'standard' language practices? Finally, how might comics be used pedagogically to help foster students' critical thinking skills and question institutional, political, and social discourses? Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Migration Ecocriticism Social justice and political activism Gender and sexuality Comics and memory studies Class, labour, and economic inequality Pedagogy and second language acquisition Nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and globalization Colonial legacies, decolonial resistance/critique Monolingualism, multilingualism, and language politics Official histories, counter archives, and silenced narratives Humour, parody, satire, and subversion Submission Guidelines Please submit a 500-word abstract with a short biographical note to Liana Pshevorska at lpshevorska@wesleyan.edu and Valentina Denzel at vdenzel@msu.edu by October 15, 2026. Informal inquiries are welcome. Decisions will be communicated in November 2026. The deadline for submitting full manuscripts is February 28, 2027. Articles should be in English, approximately 8,000 words, including images, notes, and bibliography. Contributors may include up to four images, which will be factored into the overall length of the article. Each image will be counted as approximately three-quarters of a printed page, based on an estimate 400 words per page. Please note that authors are responsible for obtaining copyright permission for all included images. Documentation of permissions should be submitted alongside the manuscript.

items.title: Who Makes Holy Writing? Authority, Ritual, and Material Practice in Religious Scribal Cultures
items.excerpt: Who Makes Holy Writing? Authority, Ritual, and Material Practice in Religious Scribal Cultures This international workshop will take place from 15-17 February 2027 in Berlin . It is organised as part of the research initiative Shaping Holiness at Freie Universität Berlin in cooperation with the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin - Preußischer Kulturbesitz....
items.fullDescription: Who Makes Holy Writing? Authority, Ritual, and Material Practice in Religious Scribal Cultures This international workshop will take place from 15-17 February 2027 in Berlin . It is organised as part of the research initiative Shaping Holiness at Freie Universität Berlin in cooperation with the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin - Preußischer Kulturbesitz. Bringing together scholars from a wide range of disciplines and religious traditions, the workshop aims to foster comparative and transdisciplinary perspectives on the production of sacred writings and the people who created them. Who is entitled to write a holy text? What transforms an ordinary writer into a religious authority? Is it ritual purity, technical expertise, theological learning, artistic mastery, or moral integrity? And how do religious communities define, regulate, and negotiate these expectations? Across many religious traditions, the production of holy writings has never been understood as a purely technical activity. Whether copying Torah scrolls, Qur??ns, Buddhist sutras, biblical manuscripts, liturgical books, ritual inscriptions, or other sacred texts, scribes were expected to embody particular forms of knowledge, discipline, and religious commitment. Yet the authority of the scribe was neither fixed nor universal. It was continually shaped through ritual practice, legal norms, material expertise, communal expectations, and individual acts of devotion. This conference invites scholars to explore the making of the sacred scribe across religious traditions and historical periods. Rather than focusing exclusively on manuscripts as finished objects, we seek to examine the people who produced them and the religious, social, legal, and material worlds in which they worked. How were scribes trained? Who was permitted to write? Which bodies, gestures, emotions, intentions, and forms of knowledge were considered essential? How were mistakes corrected, authority established, and expertise transmitted? And what can marginal notes, glosses, corrections, and colophons tell us about the everyday realities of religious writing? Possible themes include, but are not limited to: Who becomes a scribe? Authority, vocation, education, apprenticeship, and the transmission of scribal knowledge. The ideal scribe. Ethical virtues, religious authority, discipline, emotions, self-cultivation, and models of exemplary scribes. Bodies of writing. Ritual purity, bodily practices, gestures, posture, voice, intention), prayer, and devotion. Writing under rules. Legal prescriptions, ritual regulations, permissions, prohibitions, correction, error, censorship, and textual authority. Craft and creativity. Calligraphy, artistic expertise, material practices, writing technologies, and the relationship between technical skill and religious legitimacy. Communities of scribes. Scriptoria, workshops, networks, patronage, collaboration, and the social organisation of religious writing. Margins of sacred writing. Glosses, annotations, corrections, ownership notes, colophons, readers' interventions, and other traces of scribal practice. Gender and religious authority. Women, lay specialists, monastic communities, hereditary scribes, and contested forms of scribal legitimacy. Cross-religious encounters and responses. Mutual perceptions, critiques, adaptations, and exchanges between religious traditions and their scribal practices; the ways such encounters shaped concepts of sacred writing, textual authority, and scribal culture. Changing scribal worlds. Scribes between manuscript and print, digital technologies. Comparative perspectives. New methodological approaches to studying scribes across religious, cultural, and disciplinary boundaries. We particularly welcome contributions that move beyond the study of individual traditions and engage with broader comparative, methodological, or theoretical questions. Papers addressing living religious traditions alongside historical case studies are equally encouraged. Submission Please submit an abstract of 300-500 words , together with a short academic biography (max. 150 words), to amartini@zedat.fu-berlin.de by 15. October . Successful applicants will be notified by 31. October. Travel expenses and accommodation will be provided for all invited speakers.

items.title: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities
items.excerpt: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative a...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. We encourage essays focused on narratives as well as submissions that explore art installations and other medial forms that address the boundary waters circulating around and through the blue humanities. Topics may include but are not limited to the following: Boundary waters that divide and connect nations, classes, and/or ecological zones Mythic, cinematic, and visual narratives of how humans and/or nonhumans are "held," migrate, or are moved through watery littorals Critical explorations like those associated with "tidalectics," a term that comes from Kamau Brathwaite, who proposed an alternative framework for literary and political engagement that is grounded in the rhythm of waves and the cyclic ebb and flow of tides "Portraits" of littoral space(s) in literature, history, myth, the visual arts, and theatrical and musical performances Exploring the significance of physical, structural, and emotional vulnerabilities and instabilities within littorals, shoals, or port cities Hydrological infrastructure (colonial, postcolonial, urban, rural) associated with port cities, canal locks, and dams Relational undercurrents that speak to our ways of submerging ourselves into the watery worlds that surround us Traditional water ways: ways of being with or "holding" water The role of inland waterways in routing stories and/or facilitating/impeding human and nonhuman migrations Exploring the agency of oceans and rivers in sustaining capitalist and imperial economies and their alternatives Water's many forms (snow, ice, fog, rivers, oceans) and ways "water" facilitates connection and/or imposes isolation How waterways-"paths" of water and ways of being with water-lead us to new or alternative futures Scenes of erosion that expose lost or forgotten histories Please direct questions to the special issue editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri [edkunkur@mtu.edu] and Dana Van Kooy [drvankoo@mtu.edu] For questions about the use and disclosure of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, please see NANO's AI Statement (https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Journal-Information) Please use the Submission Form on top left of the CFP page: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Submissions/Submission-Form NANO: New American Notes Online is a free, open-access, peer-reviewed journal. NANO does not charge for submission, review, or publication. It is indexed in the MLA International Bibliography, GALE, ProQuest, and DOAJ.

items.fullDescription: Conference Theme: Beyond Repair: Reconciliations, Restorations, Resurgences Conference Dates: February 10-12, 2027 Submission Deadline: October 23, 2026 The African, African American, and Diaspora Studies Center at James Madison University invites proposals for its annual interdisciplinary conference Beyond Repair: Reconciliations, Restorations, Resurgences. The conference will be held from Wednesday, February 10 to Friday, February 12, 2027 and brings together scholars, archivists, and practitioners from a variety of overlapping and intersecting fields. Submit proposals by October 23, 2026. Repair has become one of the defining political and ethical vocabularies of our moment. Calls for reparations have generated new ways of imagining justice, accountability, and redress, while also raising questions about whether the language of repair is itself sufficient to address the enduring legacies of colonialism and slavery. This year's theme "Beyond Repair" gestures simultaneously in two directions: it evokes what may appear irreparable, but it also invites debate over what we mean by "repair" in the first place. What can it achieve? What are its limits? What lies past its horizons? What in our present condition is beyond repair, and where does this leave us for imagining a future that does justice to the past? This year's conference will be hybrid; we invite in-person and virtual presentations on all topics relevant to AAAD studies, even if not directly pertinent to the conference theme. We welcome proposals from scholars from all disciplines at any point in their scholarly careers. Proposals for individual presentations or pre-constituted panels could address, but are not limited to, topics such as the following: · Reparations and reparative structures · Post-conflict recovery · Frameworks of restorative justice · Relief and its discontents · Reconciliation and refusal · Resurgence and renewal · Community restoration · Global and transnational partnerships · Historical reckoning · Memory and forgetting · Archives and recovery · Narrative repair · Healing and health · Arts of restoration · Religious communities and social repair · Ecological restoration · Climate resilience · Land and belonging · Diasporic networks · Pedagogies of repair · Reproductive justice · Literary resurgences · Queer histories and futures · Transitional justice · Care and community · Reparative economy · Wealth and debt · Digital storytelling Please submit either a 300-word individual paper proposal or 1000-word panel proposal on the appropriate form linked below by October 23, 2026. Panel proposals must include at least three panelists. For panels, acceptance information will be sent directly to the panel organizer. Individual Paper Submission Form: https://forms.gle/rB6N9EB1MKNZAxBBA Panel Submission Form: https://forms.gle/5rCwccWXPFfxcgGw9 Further information and updates about the conference may be found at sites.lib.jmu.edu/aaadjmu. International respondents traveling to the United States in need of Visa documentation are encouraged to submit their abstracts as early as possible, ideally before September 15. International respondents will be notified on an ongoing basis after submitting their proposal. US respondents will be notified within a month after the deadline. Questions may be sent to aaadstudies@jmu.edu.

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. items.fullDescription: What is the real difference between speaking with nature and speaking for it? Is eco-centric thought a universally shared ideology, or does it develop in reaction to historical, philosophical, and socio-cultural contexts? In what way do the fundamental principles of Indian ecology vary from prevailing Western structures? These essential inquiries delineate the parameters of Ramachandra Guha’s Speaking with Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism (2024), which effectively contests the notion that environmentalism is a unidirectional phenomenon dictated by Western influence. This view posits that the rest of the world, particularly the Global South, lacks eco-conscious awareness because it is ‘too poor to be green’.

items.location: University of Tübingen, Germany · Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate
items.excerpt: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it e...
items.fullDescription: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it evokes and reflects basic constituents of human communication: in particular, the relationship between what is said and what is meant and the relationship between what is said and what is known. Irony comes into play when these relationships are marked by significant discrepancies. The discrepancy between what is said and what is meant is essential for verbal irony and the discrepancy between what is said and what is known is fundamental to dramatic (or narrative) irony. If and how these two kinds of irony belong together, however, is a moot point and one of the questions to be addressed by our symposium. Thus the unequal distribution of knowledge (between characters and/or between characters and the reader) which marks narrative and dramatic irony may be related to the divergence which characterizes verbal irony. When Viola in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, disguised as a boy, says to Orsino: "I am all the daughters of my father's house," Orsino, who believes Viola to be a young man, must regard this statement as verbal irony on Viola's part. What is said ("daughters") is very different from what appears to be meant ("sons"). To us, the audience, however, this is a case of dramatic irony since we know that Viola is a woman and we observe Orsino's ignorance. What makes this case particularly intriguing is that here dramatic irony is not based on a discrepancy between what is said and what we know since Viola literally speaks the truth. The discrepancy arises between what we know and what is supposed to be spoken ironically. The example shows that asking about the relationship between verbal and dramatic/narrative irony entails numerous other questions that the Connotations symposium is going to address. In particular, we will ask about effects of irony, both with regard to characters and the audience. What is the added value of an ironic remark? What does it tell us about the speaker? In what way does an ironic utterance signal that there is a common ground between the communication partners? Are the inclusion and exclusion of others, i.e. those who get the ironical meaning and those who don't, similar to cases of discrepant awareness? How do we know that an utterance is meant ironically and how are we to deal with ambiguity in this respect? Can non-verbal irony markers be encoded in literary texts? Are theories of verbal irony based on notions of echo and pretence relatable to drama and fiction? We invite papers focussing on these and related questions, based on literature in English from the Middle Ages to the present. Please send an abstract (300 words max.) to the editors of Connotations at symposium2027@connotations.de by 31 October 2026

Broadly defined, the area focuses on all forms of performing and visual arts, including all musical genres, theatrical performance and performance art, performance elements in visual art, and connections between different Black expressive forms. The panels on Black Performing Arts: Sound, Movement, Image, Text will showcase interdisciplinary discussions of cultural identity, art, religion, ritual, power, image, representation, symbols and their meaning, and the social processes and systems that influence and inform the innovation, production, regulation, and consumption of Black performing arts. items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: The 2027 Conference of the Popular Culture Association (PCA) will host a special topic area on UFOs, Cryptids, Conspiracies, and the Paranormal. The organizers of the PCA's special topic on UFOs, Cryptids, Conspiracies, and the Paranormal welcome proposals for papers and presentations from an interdisciplinary range of fields, including sociology, literature, media studies, anthropology, folklore, religion, history, political science, medieval studies, rhetoric, education, and bibliography. Papers in this area will not seek to prove or disprove the reality of any of the stigmatized subjects under discussion; instead, they will explore the cultural forces at work in their origin and development, their form and content, and the audiences that receive them. Discussions of UFOs, conspiracy theories, the paranormal, and cryptozoological creatures were once relegated to the fringes of American culture; yet in the last decade, they have steadily migrated toward its center. As the belief in conspiracy theories and the paranormal becomes increasingly influential on American culture and politics, understanding these ideas, how they develop, and the subcultures that form around them is essential for understanding the trajectory of culture in the 21st century. The belief in UFOs, conspiracy theories, paranormal occurrences, and cryptozoological creatures may seem like four disparate concepts; yet, they are connected through their shared beliefs in "stigmatized knowledge," a term developed in Michael Barkun's groundbreaking 2003 monograph A Culture of Conspiracy to describe a range of ideas rejected by mainstream culture. From the belief that alien beings visit the earth to fringe science to radical politics, adherents of these subcultures regard these ways of knowing as forgotten, superseded, ignored, rejected, occulted, and/or suppressed sources of truth. Area Theme In accordance with the PCA's 2027 theme of "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture," this area of study is particularly interested in papers relating to issues of transformation, resistance, innovation, and social change. Abstracts do not need to address this theme, but papers relating to them may be grouped in thematic panels. Possible topics include (but are not limited to): UFO/UAP Disclosure as Apocalypse Ethnography of Cryptozoological Practitioners Folklore and History of Cryptids in the Boston Area Combating Conspiracy Theories in the Classroom The Rhetoric of Stigmatized Knowledge Production Disclosure or Distraction? UFOs and Politics UFOs, Conspiracy Theories, Cryptids, and the Paranormal in Popular Television UFOs, Conspiracy Theories, Cryptids, and the Paranormal in Popular Film The Legacy of JFK's Assassination Folkloristic Aspects of UFO Accounts UFO Conspiracies and the Internet: The Influence of ParaNet Legend-Tripping and Paranormal Tourism Q-Anon and American Millenarianism Intersections of Conspiracy Theories and Moral Panic Alternative Archaeology and the Suspicion of Expertise The Apocalypse and Millennial Religious Movements Cryptids and the History of Science Cryptids and American Culture Submission Guidelines Please submit an abstract with a maximum of 300 words by October 31, 2026, through the PCA website: www.pcaaca.org. If you wish to submit a panel for the conference, all presenters must submit individually through the website, and then notify the Area Chairs of their intention to present together. If you wish to submit a proposal for a roundtable, please contact the Area Chairs in advance. Upon acceptance, presenters will need to submit a brief biography so that their session chairs can introduce them. If you are not already a member of the PCA, you must join in order to submit a proposal, and presenters whose proposals are accepted must register for the conference no later than February 15, 2027. Prior to submitting, please review the full guidelines at https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines. Questions? Please contact the area chairs: Gabriel Mckee, gm95@nyu.edu Jeremy Land, jland@mclennan.edu Important Dates Open for Submissions - 1 August 2026 Submission Deadline - 31 October 2026 Travel Grant Application Due - 15 November 2026 Notified of Acceptance - 16 November 2025 Travel Grant Recipients Notified - 31 December 2026 Early Bird Registration Ends - 31 December 2026 Regular Registration Opens - 1 January 2027 Draft of Conference Program Available - 7 January 2027 Regular Registration Deadline - 31 January 2027 Final Registration Opens - 1 February 2027 All Presenters Must Be Registered - 15 February 2027 PCA Conference in Boston - 24 - 27 March 2027

items.fullDescription: PCA Annual Conference, March 24-27, 2027: Boston, Massachusetts The Collecting and Collectibles Area invites proposals exploring how "collecting" has become an embodiment of the economic, political, environmental, and digital precarities that shape contemporary popular culture. Collecting now operates as a dynamic source for epistemic production, constantly redefining how popular culture is constructed, construed, mediated, valorized, historicized, and even contested. The 2027 PCA conference theme is "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." Presenters in Collecting and Collectibles Area are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. We welcome contributions that integrate practice-based, collaborative, comparative, transnational and cross-cultural approaches and involve innovative methods, community engagement, public and digital humanities to address topics including, but not limited to: --Emerging Technologies of Collecting: AI and collecting cultures, virtual archives, NFTs and blockchain collectibles, social media collecting communities, online marketplaces and economies, smart museums, mixed- reality collections, and AI-enabled smart twins of museums --Participatory Collecting Culture: Gaming memorabilia and sports collections, comic books, manga, anime, and graphic novels, fan archives, and exclusive/ limited editions --Popular Media collecting: Film and television memorabilia, music and vinyl records, cassettes, CDs, concert and artist-branded merchandise, celebrity memorabilia, fast-food promotional premiums, licensed toys, action figure and doll sets, LEGO, and theme park merchandise -- Heritage and Transcultural collecting: counter archives and collectibles, indigenous collections, digitality and heritage preservation, migration and portable collectibles, cultural diplomacy collections -- Crisis Collecting: Climate change and at-risk collections, pandemic collecting, trauma and collecting, sustainable and ethical colleting, resilient collections, commemorative coins and medals, satirical magazines, post-collapse souvenirs, war memorabilia -- Consumer Culture and Collecting: Auctions and collector markets and communities, investment collecting, branding and nostalgic collecting, resale platforms -- Materiality of Collecting: household collectibles, stamps, travel souvenirs, and their digital adaptations We welcome individual papers, complete panels, creative presentations, and interdisciplinary collaborations. Scholars, independent researchers, graduate students, and undergraduate students are encouraged to submit. Membership in the PCA is needed to submit a proposal.
