items.fullDescription: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. Television series, films, videogames, TikTokers, podcasters, memes and other forms of digital culture reach global audiences and shape political identities and cultural imaginaries. Far from being mere entertainment, these texts have consequently become intertwined and virtually inseparable from the daily practices through which individuals get their news input and even their education. The purpose of this year's virtual conference is to open a space for the analysis of the ethical principles (or lack thereof) that seem to guide the construction, circulation and reception of public discourses within the popular culture ecosystem, including both more traditional mediums such as television and comics, but also the products that emerge from generative AI. Popular media content exists as a key source of information in public discourse and influences how we interpret contemporary political issues, how we teach and learn, and even how we exist and behave in society. Although media effects have long been proven to be negotiated rather than direct, the understanding of desirable aesthetics, mindless entertainment and the rhetoric used in political discussions have been hugely impacted by AI generated content. With this cultural media environment in mind, this virtual conference invites explorations of US popular culture through the perspective of media ethics, media literacy and aesthetics. We aim at establishing a space of discussion on the political, educational, ethical and social implications of contemporary media consumption through the analysis of US popular culture. The conference welcomes contributions that tackle the ethical dimensions and societal impact of US popular culture across a wide range of media forms and how they operate within the fragmented and algorithmically curated media ecosystem that we inhabit. We welcome analysis of both mainstream and independent productions, historical and contemporary texts, as well as emerging digital practices. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: × Media ethics and the social responsibilities of producers, platforms and audiences × Media literacy as a framework for analyzing contemporary popular culture × Popular culture as a case study for developing media literacy, ethical reasoning and critical thinking in education × The teaching potential behind popular media texts × Media effects and audience reception of US popular culture × Social media trends, influencers and memes × AI aesthetics in popular media × Polarization, misinformation, conspiracy narratives, and the circulation of disinformation through popular media × (Un)ethical representation of minorities × Political communication, civic engagement, and democratic participation through entertainment media × Representation of political and social problems in US popular culture Deadline for proposals: 1 November 2026 We accept abstract proposals for individual presentations (≈ 250 words), as well as full panels (3 presenters, ≈ 250-word description of the panel plus brief abstracts of all papers). Please, submit your abstract proposal via email at popmec.media@gmail.com as a single attachment (.doc, .docx, .odt) including name, affiliation (if any), and contact email.

items.title: New Approaches to Teaching the Gothic
items.excerpt: Diane Long Hoeveler and Tamar Heller's Approaches to Teaching Gothic Fiction: British and American Traditions (MLA Options for Teaching) was published in 2003; Anna Powell and Andrew Smith's Teaching the Gothic (Palgrave) was published in 2006. While both texts are excellent guides for teachers of the Gothic, quite a lot has happened in the twenty years s...
items.fullDescription: Diane Long Hoeveler and Tamar Heller's Approaches to Teaching Gothic Fiction: British and American Traditions (MLA Options for Teaching) was published in 2003; Anna Powell and Andrew Smith's Teaching the Gothic (Palgrave) was published in 2006. While both texts are excellent guides for teachers of the Gothic, quite a lot has happened in the twenty years since these texts appeared, not the least of which was a Gothic-infused global pandemic and the insidious rise of artificial intelligence in daily life. Academics today are and have been teaching the Gothic at a time when the world's problems - rising fascism, global conflict, climate change, the devaluation of Higher Education, among many others - make the world itself seem downright Gothic. This collection will seek to provide updated reflections, evaluations, and strategies on teaching the Gothic and utilising or creating Gothic pedagogy in the contemporary moment and beyond. Courses on or including the Gothic are taught in a wide variety of venues within and outside academia; settings include community colleges, traditional undergraduate programmes, graduate programmes, community centres, prisons and reformatories. Classrooms themselves vary greatly, from giant lecture halls to small upper-level seminars to fully online virtual spaces. Students of the Gothic come from all ages and backgrounds, and include native speakers of English and students acquiring English later in life. These contexts, venues, and audiences present different challenges for the instructor, and require unique approaches to make for successful learning experiences. We are seeking contributions from a range of scholars at different ranks and types of institutions (as well as outside of them) to present a broad understanding of the diversity of how we study and teach the Gothic today, and to provide new directions for the future. We already have interest from an academic press. Potential topics might include but are not restricted to one or a mixture of the following: Teaching the Gothic in the midst of a crisis (e.g. pandemic, war, from a distance or physically within such spaces) Teaching the Gothic outside of the university / in non-traditional settings Challenges of AI to teaching the Gothic The use of various digital platforms in teaching / student research Gothic and the archives in contemporary times What texts (and which editions) absolutely must be on any Gothic syllabus (and why)? Gothic forms (teaching beyond traditional formats, for instance) Gothic theory as pedagogy (in times of crisis particularly) Syllabus organizational strategies and rationales: Chronological? Thematic? Canon? Decolonizing the Gothic syllabus Preparing for and managing class discussions about violence, sexual violence, trauma, discrimination, or other tough topics that arise in the Gothic? Strategies for teaching a Gothic course for an audience unfamiliar with the Gothic / unfamiliar with academia / non-traditional students. Gothic and public engagement / school outreach Opportunities for service learning / personal and professional development in the Gothic course Creative forms of assessment in the Gothic classroom Neurodivergence and the Gothic Designing assignments with AI in mind Cancel culture and the Gothic Co-editors Bridget Marshall (University of Massachusetts, Lowell) and Jen Baker (University of Warwick, UK) seek abstracts of 300-500 words for chapters which will demonstrate innovative approaches to teaching the Gothic or engaging with or creating new Gothic pedagogies, particularly situated within recent contexts. We are open to a variety of forms, including case studies, reflective essays, theoretically informed essays, and other formats that can best showcase pedagogical insights. If your proposed essay includes samples of work by students/participants we will require written permissions before publication. Please also include a brief professional bio of 300 words (max) with your abstract. Please send your abstract and bio by 10 November 2026 to Bridget_Marshall@uml.edu and J.Baker.5@warwick.ac.uk We are happy to answer questions at the same address.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Volume 37, Issue 1 & 2 (2027) Dear Colleagues, Litera: Journal of Language, Literature and Culture Studies - Dil, Edebiyat ve Kültür Ara?t?rmalar? Dergisi, the official publication of the Department of Western Languages and Literatures at Istanbul University, invites submissions for its 2026 issues (Volume 36, Issues 1 & 2). An open-access, peer-reviewed, and multilingual journal published twice a year (June & December), Litera is indexed in ELSEVIER SCOPUS, Web of Science ESCI, MLA International Bibliography, DOAJ (Directory of Open Access Journals), ERIH PLUS, EBSCO Communication Source, EBSCO Central & Eastern European Academic Source, Gale Cengage and Ulrichsweb. While our core focus remains on literary studies, linguistics, and cultural studies, we welcome interdisciplinary approaches that combine literary and linguistic analysis with insights from cultural theory and media studies-provided they maintain a clear relevance to our aim and scope We welcome original research articles that engage with current debates and critical issues in the study of Western (American, English, French, Belgian, German, Swiss, Austrian, Italian, Spanish, Latin American and Modern Greek) languages, literatures, and cultures. In particular, we encourage contributions that reflect cutting-edge scholarship in areas such as, but not limited to: · Contemporary literary theory · Disability Studies · Human-Animal Studies · Posthumanism and critical posthumanities · Ecofeminism and ecocriticism · Ecosemiotics and Ecolinguistics · Discourse Studies · Intersectional and decolonial approaches · Digital humanities and media theory · Film Studies · Medieval Studies · Posthuman Communication Studies · Gender studies · Narrative and identity in contemporary fiction · Transnationalism and migration literature · Crete studies Submission Windows: · Issue 1 (June 2027): November 1-30, 2026 · Issue 2 (December 2027): May 1-31, 2027 Submission Guidelines: Manuscripts must be original, unpublished, and not under review elsewhere. Re-use of thesis content, dissertations, or previously published conference material is not permitted. All submissions are subject to a double-blind peer reviewprocess. Languages of Publication: English, German, French, Italian, and Spanish No processing or publication fees. Eligibility: Submissions are accepted from authors who hold a PhD. For more information, visit our journal homepage. We look forward to receiving your innovative and thought-provoking research. Sincerely, Editorial Team Litera: Journal of Language, Literature and Culture Studies

items.fullDescription: 2027 marks the 50th anniversary of the film now generally known as Episode IV: A New Hope , the first instalment in the hugely successful Star Wars franchise created by George Lucas. As beloved as it is divisive, Star Wars now straddles multiple decades and generations while proliferating across narrative media (novels, comics, games, animation, TV). It provides a series of compelling case studies in the relationship between creativity and commerce, from the foundation of Lucasfilm during the New Hollywood period to the 21st century Disney-era, and it has developed via a complex interplay between cutting-edge technological innovation, nostalgia, and mythmaking.

items.excerpt: In her book Bodyminds Reimagined , Sami Schalk asks us “What might it mean to imagine disability differently?” (2) Her work, situated in the exploration of black speculative fiction, engages with (dis)ability studies and black feminism to gesture toward a reimagining of what Margaret Price termed the ‘bodymind’, a concept predicated on “the enmeshment of...
items.fullDescription: In her book Bodyminds Reimagined , Sami Schalk asks us “What might it mean to imagine disability differently?” (2) Her work, situated in the exploration of black speculative fiction, engages with (dis)ability studies and black feminism to gesture toward a reimagining of what Margaret Price termed the ‘bodymind’, a concept predicated on “the enmeshment of the mind and body.” (5) How might this enmeshment be understood in the context of chronic conditions, themselves experienced as a direct result of climate change and biomedical violence? Is the planet - made sick by extractive capitalism and anthropogenic action as Shukla, Settee, Lincoln and others claim - now existing in a state of (dis)ability?

items.title: Modern Meta Myths
items.excerpt: We are seeking chapter proposals for a new edited collection entitled Modern Meta Myths, examining intersections of mythic adaptation/reception with critical self-awareness. The collection aims to bring together a diverse array of chapters, working through different methodologies, generic focuses, and analyzing adaptations/receptions of various world myth...
items.fullDescription: We are seeking chapter proposals for a new edited collection entitled Modern Meta Myths, examining intersections of mythic adaptation/reception with critical self-awareness. The collection aims to bring together a diverse array of chapters, working through different methodologies, generic focuses, and analyzing adaptations/receptions of various world mythological traditions. We define "myth" broadly, to include legends, fairy tales, religious stories, even folk tales, in addition to more traditional bodies of mythology. In particular, we're excited to read proposals about world mythic engagement beyond the Euro-American tradition. Meta- self-awareness is central to twentieth and twenty-first century literary and artistic styles, as Modernists, Postmodernists, and Metamodernists navigate new ways of engaging the past and our shared cultural and historical heritages. This collection specifically intends to explore ways in which authors/artists in these contemporary traditions figure the meanings and cultural work of mythology. Examining these intersections is the collection's critical intervention, setting it apart from other works in the broad field of adaptation and reception studies. MMM will be divided into two broad sections. One section will examine meta-mythic adaptations/receptions of chapters focused on texts/art commenting on or critiquing the nature and cultural work of mythology or a specific myth. The other section will focus on adaptations/receptions foregrounding meta-genre elements-e.g., fiction that's conscious of itself as fiction, cinema that points to the cinematic process, drama addressing the nature of live performance, etc. Strong chapter proposals should: include a provisional thesis statement, specify the myth(s) and adaptation(s) being examined, the meta- element the chapter will analyze (whether that's meta-mythic or meta-generic), the critical lens(es) being utilized, and set the stakes for this argument. Tell us why your chapter's argument matters. Why would someone want to pick up MMM and read your work? We welcome chapters that address topics like (but not exclusively): Post-colonial or de-colonial explorations of Indigenous, African, Latin American, Asian, Polynesian, etc. identity through critical engagement with mythology Intercultural adaptation/reception Generic differences in trans-medial adaptations (e.g., epic poetry to film, folk story to novel) Multi-media/multi-genre works Weaving together multiple mythic traditions, particularly from different cultural traditions Feminist engagement with and critique of myth Explorations of cultural power imbalances preserved by myth, and attempts to use myth to challenge those imbalances So far, Bloomsbury, McFarland, and Palgrave have expressed preliminary interest in publishing the project, and we are waiting to hear from or in discussion with other publishers who publish on adaptation and reception studies. Please email a 200-300 word chapter proposal, four-five keywords, and short bio and/or brief CV to modernmetamyths@gmail.com by 31 Dec. 2026. Acceptance decisions will be made and announced in early Jan. 2027. Drafts of accepted chapters will provisionally be due by 31 Dec. 2027. Chapters should generally be between 6,000-8,000 words (exclusive of notes and citations). Please use 9th edition MLA format for citations (both in-text and Works Cited lists), though the citation format may be changed based on the publishers' house style.

items.fullDescription: The International Journal of English Literature, Social Sciences, and Multidisciplinary Studies (IJELS) publishes original research papers, review articles, and case studies that advance scholarly knowledge across English literature, social sciences, and multidisciplinary studies. The journal provides a global platform for researchers, educators, and professionals to share innovative ideas, critical analyses, and interdisciplinary perspectives. Submission open to Current Issue Feedback Notification: within 1 Month after submission (Online Peer Review System) IJELS welcomes high-quality submissions on a broad range of topics, including but not limited to: English Literature and Language Studies - English literature, world literature, comparative literature, interdisciplinary approaches to literature, literature and media, critical theory, English language teaching and learning, communicative language teaching (CLT), task-based language teaching (TBLT), second language acquisition, English language testing and assessment, syllabus design and curriculum development, applied linguistics, corpus linguistics, discourse analysis, translation studies, English globalization, and English-speaking cultures. Social Sciences and Humanities - Anthropology, Sociology, Psychology, Political Science, Economics, Education, Geography, History, Law, International Relations, Criminology, Public Administration, Development Studies, Human Rights, Social Welfare, Gender Studies, and Ethics. Arts and Cultural Studies - Performing Arts (music, theatre, and dance), Visual Arts, Cultural and Cross-Cultural Studies, Media Studies, Communication Studies, and Philosophy. Business, Law, and Information Studies - Business Studies, Corporate Governance, Industrial Relations, Information Science, Library Science, and Paralegal Studies. Multidisciplinary Studies - Research that bridges multiple academic disciplines to address complex social, cultural, linguistic, educational, technological, or global challenges. IJELS particularly values cross-cutting studies that integrate methodologies and perspectives from different fields to generate new insights and foster innovation. IJELS encourages diverse theoretical, empirical, and methodological approaches that promote intellectual exchange and interdisciplinary collaboration, fostering research at the dynamic intersection of literature, language, social sciences, and multidisciplinary inquiry. You may submit your article to: ijels.infogain@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - VI Convegno Internazionale "Lingua, Letteratura, Vino e Territorio" ITALIANO VI Convegno Internazionale Lingua, Letteratura, Vino e Territorio «Egli è il vero oro potabile, / che mandar suole in esilio / ogni male inrimediabile» - Francesco Redi, Il Bacco in Toscana Università di Padova, Italia - 9-11 giugno 2027 L'Università di Padova annuncia il call for papers del VI Convegno Internazionale Lingua, Letteratura, Vino e Territorio, che si terrà dal 9 all'11 giugno 2027. Questa sesta edizione desidera riunire studiosi e ricercatori operanti in università, centri di ricerca e altre istituzioni con una consolidata tradizione legata al vino, che vogliano presentare le loro riflessioni intorno alle linee tematiche proposte. Il convegno ambisce a essere un punto d'incontro e a creare sinergie fra istituzioni e regioni vitivinicole che coltivino allo stesso tempo l'interesse e lo studio per la lingua, la letteratura e le altre discipline umanistiche. Il vino, nella tradizione letteraria italiana e romanza, non occupa infatti il ruolo di una semplice bevanda, ma si presenta come un oggetto culturale prismatico, capace di rappresentare l'identità di un territorio. Le proposte potranno inserirsi nelle seguenti linee di ricerca: La lingua e il discorso intorno al vino. La cultura del vino nella letteratura, nell'arte e nella storia. Linguaggi del vino: tradizione testuale, lessico, terminologia e traduzione. Territorio, società, economia e turismo enologico. Il convegno è multilingue. Sono ammesse comunicazioni in italiano, francese, spagnolo, portoghese e inglese. Invio delle proposte Le proposte di comunicazione dovranno pervenire entro il 31 dicembre 2026 e dovranno contenere: titolo della comunicazione; abstract di massimo 250 parole e cinque parole chiave; breve nota biografica dell'autore di massimo 150 parole. Ciascun intervento avrà una durata massima di 20 minuti. Tutte le proposte saranno valutate in forma anonima dal Comitato scientifico. Gli autori riceveranno comunicazione dell'accettazione entro il 31 gennaio 2027. Le proposte devono essere inviate a: convegno.vino.padova2027@gmail.com Quote di iscrizione Studiosi strutturati - professori e ricercatori 130 € con iscrizione entro il 20 febbraio 2027; 160 € con iscrizione entro il 31 marzo 2027. Giovani studiosi non strutturati - dottorandi e post-doc 80 € con iscrizione entro il 20 febbraio 2027; 110 € con iscrizione entro il 31 marzo 2027. Uditori con certificato di partecipazione: 30 €. La quota di iscrizione comprende inoltre la partecipazione a eventi culturali a tema vino previsti nell'ambito del convegno. ENGLISH 6th International Conference Language, Literature, Wine and Territory "Egli è il vero oro potabile, / che mandar suole in esilio / ogni male inrimediabile" - Francesco Redi, Il Bacco in Toscana University of Padua, Italy - June 9-11, 2027 The University of Padua announces the call for papers for the 6th International Conference Language, Literature, Wine and Territory, to be held on June 9-11, 2027. This sixth edition of the International Conference aims to bring together scholars and researchers working in universities, research centres, and other institutions with a well-established tradition linked to wine, who wish to present their reflections on the proposed thematic lines. The conference aspires to be a meeting point and to create synergies between institutions and wine-producing regions that foster an interest in language, literature, and the humanities. In the Italian and Romance literary tradition, wine does not merely play the role of a simple beverage, but stands as a multifaceted cultural object capable of representing the identity of a territory. Proposals are invited within the following research lines: Language and discourse about wine. Wine culture in literature, art, and history. Languages of wine: textual tradition, lexicon, terminology, and translation. Territory, society, economy, and wine tourism. The conference is multilingual. Papers may be presented in Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, or English. Submission of proposals Paper proposals must be received by December 31, 2026, and must include: title; abstract of no more than 250 words and five keywords; short biographical note of the author of no more than 150 words. Each presentation must not exceed 20 minutes. All proposals will be evaluated anonymously by the Scientific Committee. Authors will receive notification of acceptance by January 31, 2027. Proposals should be sent to: convegno.vino.padova2027@gmail.com Registration fees Full and Associate Professors / established researchers €130 when registering by February 20, 2027; €160 when registering by March 31, 2027. Early-career researchers - PhD students and post-docs €80 when registering by February 20, 2027; €110 when registering by March 31, 2027. Attendees without a presentation, with participation certificate: €30. The registration fee also includes participation in wine-related cultural events organised as part of the conference programme. items.fullDescription: How is everyone doing? At a routine meeting of the Editorial Board of this journal in March 2026, this innocuous question erupted into disquiet, tension, unease. Speaking from vastly different parts of the world, there was an unmistakable sense of a planet slipping beyond available comprehension and unplugging us from work and life routines. As wars in the Middle East expand and fires spread from apartment blocks reduced to rubble to bombed oil refineries and shipping corridors, profound geopolitical, personal, even psychic rifts leave us grasping for the language and feel of the moment, the falling apart of things, the zeitgeist of an endangered now.

items.fullDescription: The advancement of artificial intelligence has transformed humanities research and education, deepening computation’s influence on scholarly practice and everyday life. From the early era of “humanities computing” in the 1970s to the rise of “computational humanities” over the past decade, this trajectory highlights the enduring—and expanding—role of computation in shaping inquiry across the humanities. These intersections are especially visible in interdisciplinary work. As T. S. Eliot observes, “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal; bad poets deface what they take, and good poets make it into something better, or at least something different.” The same spirit can illuminate how methods and tools migrate across fields.

items.fullDescription: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth, a production requiring expansiveness in its sustained attention (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities and identifications, and it cuts against the second half of his title, which suggests Blackness in terms of negation, evasion, and minimization. The title to this conference continues a conversation with Riggs and also with Ralph Ellison, Ama Ata Aidoo, Toni Morrison, Stuart Hall, and centuries of international Black thought. By doubling down on the "is" and considering contradictory, harmonious, and contrapuntal accounts of the many ways Blackness is and can be, the Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association hopes to encourage a maximalist exchange with its conference, being held March 25-26, 2027, as a contemplation of storytelling and its connections to productions and identities of Blackness. We also seek to do commemorative work as we honor the career of Dr. Jimisha Relerford, a graduate of our program and member of the Howard community who passed recently. Her dissertation broke critical ground in its study of Black women's satire. We thus encourage the submission of papers about Black satire, especially Black women's work in the genre. Writers such as Leone Ross, Danzy Senna, Fran Ross, and Zadie Smith, all of whom were discussed in Dr. Relerford's dissertation, utilize satire to comment on and transform notions of Blackness. We hope to continue Dr. Relerford's work by contemplating how storytellers work within this genre to talk about identity. We additionally encourage work on Afrofuturism and speculative Black texts in reference to our organization's namesake, a pillar in Afrofuturist study. In addition to recognizing the intellectual impacts of Drs. Relerford and Hampton, this conference serves as a milestone, marking the tenth conference our organization has hosted in honor of Black literary study. Given Black academia and HBCUs's influence on identity and storytelling around it, we also welcome papers grounded in studies of scholarly impacts on identity as seen in multimodal narratives, productions, protests, and criticism. We additionally invite papers in the following areas that intersect with identity and identification study in story: African Studies African-American Studies Caribbean Studies Disability Studies Ecocriticism and Ecopoetics Diaspora, Ethnicity, and Migration Studies Food Studies Hip Hop Humor Literary History Protest and Rhetoric Queer Studies Television and Film To submit a paper or panel to our conference, please email an abstract of 250-300 words to gesasecretary@gmail.com no later than January 15, 2027. Include in your email, your name, affiliation, contact information, and a brief biographical blurb.

items.title: Frames and Framing: Constructing Meaning in Literature, Linguistics, and Translation
items.location: Faculty of Al-Alsun (Languages), Ain Shams University
items.excerpt: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, f...
items.fullDescription: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, frames are negotiated, shifted, and sometimes shattered in the movement between languages and cultures. They are the selective filters that highlight certain elements while relegating others to the background, the conceptual structures that allow us to categorize, interpret, and communicate complex realities.

items.fullDescription: Information, Medium & Society: Twenty-Fifth International Conference on Publishing Studies, University of Split, Croatia, 30 June - 2 July 2027 Information, Medium & Society: The Publishing Studies Research Network was founded in 2003 with the inaugural International Conference on the Future of the Book. Since then, the Research Network has expanded its scope in two phases. The first was in 2009 when it became the Books, Publishing, and Libraries Research. In this iteration, the Research Network began to look beyond the book as the primary site of investigation. In 2019 the network underwent another change, to become Information, Medium & Society - The Publishing Studies Research Network. Information, Medium & Society: Twenty-Fifth International Conference on Publishing Studies will address the following annual themes and special focus: 2027 Special Focus-Mediated Worlds: Platforms, Infrastructures, and the Making of Social Reality Theme 1: Editorial Judgment, Trust, and Knowledge Authority Theme 2: Platforms, Infrastructures, and Publishing Workflows Theme 3: Libraries, Archives, and Knowledge Stewardship Theme 4: Access, Sustainability, and the Political Economy of Publishing Theme 5: Automation, AI, and the Mediation of Knowledge

items.fullDescription: Twenty-Fifth International Conference on New Directions in the Humanities, University of Split, Croatia, 30 June - 2 July 2027 Founded in 2003, the New Directions in the Humanities Research Network is brought together by a common interest in established traditions in the humanities while at the same time developing innovative practices and setting a renewed agenda for their future. We seek to build an epistemic community where we can make linkages across disciplinary, geographic, and cultural boundaries. As a Research Network, we are defined by our scope and concerns and motivated to build strategies for action framed by our shared themes and tensions. Twenty-Fifth International Conference on New Directions in the Humanities will address the following annual themes and special focus: 2027 Special Focus-Archipelagos of Meaning: Humanities in a World of Many Worlds Theme 1: Engaged Humanities, Citizenship, and Democratic Culture Theme 2: Language, Power, and Meaning-Making Theme 3: Literature, Narrative, and Cultural Imagination Theme 4: Technologies of Communication: AI, Media, and Interpretation Theme 5: Place, Community, and Sustainable Futures

items.fullDescription: XXXIV Congreso Internacional sobre Aprendizaje, Universidad Aristóteles de Tesalónica, Grecia, 7-9 de julio de 2027. Fundada en 1989, la Red de Investigación de Aprendizaje se reúne en torno a un interés común por el aprendizaje ?en sus vertientes tanto formal como informal? abarcando todos sus niveles: desde el aprendizaje durante la primera infancia, pasando por el periodo escolar, enseñanza secundaria y universitaria, hasta la educación para adultos que se desarrolla en las diferentes poblaciones y ámbitos laborales. El XXXIV Congreso Internacional sobre Aprendizaje invita a presentar investigaciones que abordan los siguientes temas anuales y el tema destacado de 2027: Tema destacado 2027 - Educación democrática en la era de la IA: Diversidad y alfabetización para la IA Tema 1: Futuros democráticos del aprendizaje Tema 2: Diversidad crítica e inclusión Tema 3: Aprendizaje práctico de la IA Tema 4: Gobernanza y ética en la educación
